sentences.text: Yes, a dedicated discharge coordinator improved some aspects of discharge quality, though the evidence is mixed by outcome.

In an intervention study of 600 randomly sampled adult medical patients discharged home from three medical wards, adding a discharge coordinator improved the discharge planning process, reduced problems patients experienced after discharge, and reduced perceived need for medical and healthcare services.
However, it did not improve timely or effective provision of community services after discharge or the appropriateness/efficiency of bed use.
A separate survey study concerned discharge information and coordination-of-care composites, not a dedicated discharge coordinator.

No, the evidence suggests the Barthel Index alone is not an adequate measure of long-term outcome after stroke, because it correlates only modestly or weakly with several quality-of-life and handicap measures.
In a cross-sectional follow-up of 106 first-ever stroke patients (median age 71, mean 4.9 years post-stroke) in south east London, Barthel scores were compared with multiple scales.

Correlations with SF-36 dimensions ranged from r=0.217 (role emotional) to r=0.810 (physical functioning), with the Nottingham Health Profile from r=-0.189 (sleep, NS) to r=-0.840 (physical mobility), and with life satisfaction r=0.361, HADS depression r=-0.563, London handicap r=0.726, and Frenchay activities r=0.826.
Another cohort study used the Barthel Index as a primary outcome at 12 months but did not assess whether it alone is sufficient.
The evidence is mixed: oral endotracheal intubation efficacy in the helicopter environment was impaired in terms of speed but not in success rate.

In a BO-105 helicopter, flight nurses performing manikin intubations took significantly longer in-flight (25.9 ± 10.9 seconds) than on an emergency department stretcher (13.2 ± 2.8 seconds) (ANOVA, p<.001).
All control intubations were correctly placed in the trachea, whereas two (6.7%) in-flight intubations were esophageal, but this difference was not significant (chi2=0.3; p>0.05).
Yes, low serum chloride level appears to be a risk factor for cardiovascular mortality.

In a 10-year follow-up of 4793 men and 4313 women aged 25-74 free of symptomatic coronary heart disease at baseline, serum chloride level was one of the strongest independent predictors of CVD mortality.
The adjusted risk ratio for CVD death among subjects with serum chloride ≤100 mmol/l compared with those above that limit was 1.65 (95% CI 1.06-2.57) for men and 2.16 (95% CI 1.11-4.22) for women.
The study also found a decreasing log-linear dose-response relation between baseline serum chloride and total and cardiovascular mortality.
Yes, the PET data indicate amoxapine meets the receptor-occupancy criteria for atypical antipsychotics.

In seven healthy volunteers given 50-250 mg/day amoxapine for 5 days, 5-HT2 receptors were near saturated at doses of 100 mg/day and above, D2 occupancy never exceeded 80%, and 5-HT2 occupancy exceeded D2 occupancy at all doses.
These findings match the supplied atypical antipsychotic profile of high 5-HT2 occupancy, greater 5-HT2 than D2 occupancy, and EPS risk primarily when D2 occupancy exceeds 80%.

Yes, the evidence indicates that perforation of the appendix is a risk factor for tubal infertility, with appendectomy also associated with ectopic pregnancy, though methodological limitations weaken the evidence.

A systematic review of four controlled studies found risk estimates ranging from 1.6 (95% CI 1.1–2.5) for ectopic pregnancy after appendectomy to 4.8 (95% CI 1.5–14.9) for tubal infertility from appendiceal perforation.
However, recall bias and poor adjustment for confounding variables in some reports weakened the validity of these findings.
No—variations in carotid endarterectomy (CEA) use were not explained by population need in the supplied population-level analysis.

Across district populations in two English health regions, utilisation varied 14-fold, but CEA rates showed no association with district stroke mortality (r=-0.06, 95% CI -0.41 to 0.30) or stroke admission rates (r=0.17, 95% CI -0.2 to 0.49).
Instead, higher utilisation was strongly related to residence in districts where services were located, and rates were lowest in the most affluent wards.
No, clinician assessment for acute chest syndrome (ACS) in febrile patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) is not accurate enough, because physician sensitivity for predicting ACS was only 39%.
In a prospective study of 73 SCD patients with 96 febrile events, 24% (23/96) had CXR evidence of ACS, but 61% (14/23) of ACS cases were not clinically suspected before CXR.
No symptom or physical examination finding except splinting helped identify ACS, and 57% of patients with ACS had completely normal physical examination findings.
Diagnostic accuracy did not improve significantly with increasing levels of pediatric training.
Yes, laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery appears feasible in a case series of 46 consecutive patients at two academic medical centers.
In that series, laparoscopic reoperative procedures were completed with a 20% overall conversion rate to open surgery, which fell to 0% in the last 10 patients, and 0% mortality.

The mean hospital stay for laparoscopically completed operations was 2.3 +/- 0.9 days, and among 35 patients followed for 17.2 +/- 11.8 months, 31 (89%) were satisfied with their decision to have reoperation.
The other supplied passage concerns quality of life after primary laparoscopic antireflux surgery for patient preference and does not address reoperation for failed antireflux surgery.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether desflurane alters left ventricular function specifically during aortic surgery.

In a study of 50 patients scheduled for vascular surgery, 16 developed hypertension at surgical incision; desflurane controlled systolic arterial pressure in all 16, and no change was noted in heart rate, cardiac index, mean pulmonary arterial pressure, stroke volume, end-diastolic and end-systolic cross-sectional areas, fractional area change, or left ventricular circumferential fiber shortening.
However, that study enrolled vascular surgery patients, not specifically aortic surgery, so it does not directly answer the question for aortic surgery.
Yes—the evidence indicates the NIHSS favors left-hemisphere strokes, because right-sided strokes tend to have larger volumes for the same score.

In 153 acute stroke patients, those with NIHSS 0–5 had greater DWI lesion volumes for right than left strokes (mean 8.8 vs 3.2 cm3, P=0.04), and among lesions larger than 9 cm3, 8 of 37 right-sided strokes versus 1 of 39 left-sided strokes had NIHSS 0–5 (P=0.01); adjusted analysis also found lower acute NIHSS on the right for a given stroke volume (P=0.03).

In the NINDS t-PA placebo arm, right hemisphere stroke volume was greater than left after adjusting for baseline NIHSS (P<0.001), with right strokes roughly double the median volume of left strokes in each 5-point NIHSS category below 20 (e.g., NIHSS 16–20: 48 mL left vs 133 mL right, P<0.001).
Yes—the evidence indicates that MQSA implementation was associated with improved mammography quality in North Carolina.
All mammography facilities were inspected during 1993–1994 and again in 1995, and the percentage meeting quality standards increased from the first to the second inspection.
Specifically, phantom image passing rose from 31.6% to 78.2%, darkroom fog passing from 74.3% to 88.5%, and developer temperature difference passing from 62.4% to 86.9%.
Yes, an observational study found that ST-segment ischaemic events were significantly associated with preceding hypotensive events in patients with ischaemic heart disease on hypotensive medications.

In 25 such patients, 107 hypotensive events were documented; 40 ST events occurred in 14 patients, and 14 hypotension-induced ischaemia events occurred in 8 patients, with 13 of 14 preceded by a fall in diastolic pressure and 6 by a fall in systolic pressure (chi2=11.9, p<0.001).

ST events were significantly associated with preceding hypotensive events (chi2=40.2, p<0.0001), and patients with these events were more often taking multiple hypotensive drug regimens (8/8 vs 9/17, p=0.022).
This observational evidence shows association but not definitive causation, and the other supplied passages do not address whether hypotensive events cause ischaemic events.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient to say prophylaxis in all hospitalised medical patients makes sense, because the supplied passages show non-uniform risk and do not directly compare universal versus targeted prophylaxis outcomes.

In a general internal ward, symptomatic venous thrombosis occurred in 39/6332 (0.6%) patients, with incidence 2.7% in those with known malignancy versus 0.3% (15/5456) in those without, and a relative risk of 10.0 (95% CI 5.3-18.9) due to malignancy.
One proposed protocol assumes VTE risk is present for all patients and uses contraindications to guide prophylaxis instead of risk stratification, but no outcome data are reported.
Another source states it is difficult to prescribe prophylaxis systematically for cancer patients with central venous catheters and that higher-risk patients must be identified.
Thus the passages do not settle the question; they show low overall incidence but much higher risk with malignancy, with some support for universal risk assumption and some for targeting.

The evidence is insufficient to say abdominal CT is always necessary in intoxicated blunt trauma patients; the only directly relevant supplied study found a low but nonzero injury rate in a low-risk subgroup.

Among 324 intoxicated blunt trauma patients with blood alcohol ≥80 mg/dL, GCS 15, and an unremarkable abdominal examination, 317 (98%) had negative abdominal CT, 7 (2%) had abdominal injuries, and only 2 (0.6%) required abdominal exploration.
Because 2% still had injuries and major chest injury was associated with abdominal injury, these data do not prove that CT can be safely omitted.
No, the evidence from the supplied study does not support a role for antiphospholipid antibodies as risk factors for avascular necrosis of bone in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.

In a cohort of 265 SLE patients followed from 1978 to 1998, 11 patients had AVN, giving a point prevalence of 4%, and there were no significant differences in individual antiphospholipid antibodies (IgM and IgG anticardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant) or their combination between the AVN group and two control groups.

The study specifically aimed to investigate antiphospholipid antibody status with adjustment for corticosteroid use as risk factors for AVN, and it matched AVN patients for age, sex, ethnicity, duration of disease, and organ disease with two other SLE patients.

The other supplied passages address antiphospholipid antibody specificity for aPL-related events or the prevalence and correlation of aCL and aPS isotypes with SLE manifestations, but they do not provide data on AVN.
Yes, head positioning influences anterior chamber depth in pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

In 39 patients with clinically apparent unilateral pseudoexfoliation and elevated intraocular pressure, central anterior chamber depth decreased from a mean of 3.08 mm supine to 2.95 mm prone in pseudoexfoliation eyes, versus 3.01 mm to 2.97 mm in fellow eyes.
The prone-position decrease was significantly greater in pseudoexfoliation eyes than in fellow eyes, while intraocular pressure and axial length did not differ significantly between positions.
No—among patients with Werlhof's disease undergoing cardiac surgery with extracorporeal circulation, a case-control study found bleeding outcomes similar to matched controls without WD.
In 10 WD patients versus matched no-WD controls, total mediastinal drainage was almost identical (1140 mL vs 1197 mL), and one patient in each group required reexploration for bleeding.

However, WD patients had significantly lower platelet counts and received more platelet concentrates (mean 2.3 vs 0.7, P=0.007), so the evidence suggests no clear increase in clinical bleeding complications but is limited by the small sample.
Yes—open-access endoscopy was associated with less adequate pre-procedure information than GI subspecialty clinic referral, though it does not show that patients received no information.

In outpatients presenting for upper or lower endoscopy, open-access patients reported significantly less information to help identify the procedure (p<0.01) and less explanation of the procedure's nature (p<0.005) than patients referred from a GI subspecialty clinic.

Satisfaction did not differ for conscious-sedation examinations, but GI clinic patients were more satisfied with unsedated flexible sigmoidoscopy, and most patients received results from a gastroenterologist rather than the referring physician.
The other supplied studies address appropriateness, guidelines, and endoscopic findings in open-access referral, not informed consent.
No, the supplied evidence suggests amblyopic visual loss is not necessarily permanent, based on improvement in amblyopic eyes after intervention or observation.

In a series of 12 cases, nine with a history of amblyopia showed improvement, with mean distance and near acuity gains of 3.3 and 1.9 logMAR lines by 12 months, generally occurring between 1 and 12 months and remaining stable over follow-up.
Treatment approaches for children with unilateral amblyopia include refractive correction and occlusion, implying potential for visual recovery.
However, these passages do not compare treated versus untreated amblyopia or report long-term permanence, so they do not show that all amblyopic visual loss is reversible.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether pulmonary valve replacement in adults late after repair of tetralogy of Fallot is being performed too late.

Chronic pulmonary regurgitation after tetralogy repair leads to right ventricular dilation and an increased incidence of sudden cardiac death in adults , which supports concern about late intervention, but no supplied passage compares early versus late PVR or reports outcomes by timing.
One small study of mechanical valved conduit PVR included 14 patients (7 with tetralogy of Fallot) with a mean of 3.0 previous operations and reported only short-term results.
Therefore the passages show the rationale for PVR but do not answer whether the timing is too late.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether folic acid must be continued long term, but it shows that stopping folic acid for up to 1 year increased toxicity in RA patients established on methotrexate <20 mg weekly and folic acid 5 mg daily.

In a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 75 such patients, 17 (46%) placebo patients versus 8 (21%) continuing folic acid stopped the study early (P=0.02), two placebo patients discontinued because of neutropenia, and at 9 months nausea was more frequent with placebo (45% vs 7%, P=0.001).
Because follow-up lasted only 1 year, these data support continuing folic acid in the medium term but do not directly answer the long-term requirement.
No—in the one supplied study of general medical outpatients, patients with medically unexplained symptoms were not more alexithymic overall.

That cross-sectional internal medicine outpatient study found that 169 of 321 patients had unexplained symptoms according to two independent raters; they more often had a mental disorder but did not differ overall on alexithymia.

Alexithymia was also not associated with subjective health experience or medical service use in the unexplained-symptom group, although a subgroup with both unexplained symptoms and a mental disorder who denied any emotional-physical connection had more alexithymic traits.
Because this evidence is cross-sectional, it does not establish alexithymia as a temporal risk factor.
Other supplied data link alexithymia to increased reporting of medically unexplained symptoms in students and anxiety-treatment patients, not general medical outpatients.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that antral follicle assessment is a better predictor than age and FSH, though it appears to add independent predictive information.

In 224 IVF patients, baseline antral follicle >6 vs ≤6 was associated with a significantly higher clinical pregnancy rate (51% vs 19%), and this remained significant after controlling for patient age and basal FSH.
Cancellation rate was also significantly higher with antral follicle ≤6 vs ≥6 (33% vs 1%) and increased with advancing maternal age and elevated basal FSH.

The supplied passages do not directly compare the predictive strength of antral follicle assessment against age or FSH, and other passages address miscarriage, OHSS, or AMH/IUI outcomes rather than this comparison.

No—the evidence suggests the APACHE II score is not a reliable marker of physiological impairment in emergency surgical patients because it is not independent of treatment effects and its ICU-admission value overpredicted mortality. In 85 consecutive emergency surgical ICU patients, the mean APACHE II score increased from 17.8 ± 7.7 before surgery to 24.2 ± 8.3 at ICU admission (~36% higher, P<.001); the initial score predicted 34% mortality versus 32% observed, but the ICU-admission score predicted 50% mortality versus 32% observed (P=.02). Other supplied passages do not settle this question: one studied SAPS II rather than APACHE II in surgical ICU patients , and another found only a weak positive correlation between APACHE II and frailty index (r=0.190, p=0.036) in a general ICU cohort.
No — the supplied evidence suggests managed care does not enable more low-income persons to have a usual source of care, and may reduce it for some groups.

In a nationally representative sample of 14,271 low-income persons surveyed in 1996–1997, high community managed care penetration was associated with a lower likelihood of having a usual source of care for uninsured persons (54.8% vs.
62.2% in low-penetration areas) and a lower likelihood of having a usual physician (60% vs.
Managed care had only marginal effects on having a usual source of care for privately insured and Medicaid beneficiaries.
The other supplied passage does not address managed care or low-income persons' usual source of care.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether patient position during liver surgery influences the risk of venous air embolism.

In 10 patients during liver surgery, positioning at horizontal, 20 degrees head-up, and 20 degrees head-down changed absolute central and hepatic venous pressures, being highest head-down and lowest head-up, but produced no demonstrable hepatic-to-central venous pressure gradient and no negative intraluminal pressure at any time.
This study addresses a physiological surrogate rather than actual venous air embolism events, so it does not settle the clinical question.
The other supplied passages address trauma, portal vein embolization, or intrahepatic air during liver transplantation and do not address patient position during liver surgery.
Yes, the manic/mixed episode distinction appears to run true over time.

In an 11-year study of 241 bipolar disorder patients with three or more entries in a community mental health center management information system, the observed distribution of 1,224 manic and mixed episodes was compared with an expected distribution from 1,000 random simulations.
Episodes were consistent (all manic or all mixed) in significantly more patients than would be expected by chance.
The other supplied passages do not directly test this longitudinal consistency.
Yes—outcome in children with malignancy who develop acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) can be predicted from respiratory parameters.
In a retrospective review of 17 mechanically ventilated children with ARDS and malignancy (mean age 10.5 ± 5.1 years), 6 of 17 (35.3%) survived and sepsis syndrome was present in 70.6%.

Peak inspiratory pressure, positive end-expiratory pressure, and ventilation index values could distinguish outcome by day 3, while oxygenation efficiency (PaO2/FIO2 and P(A-a)O2) related significantly to outcome from day 8 after mechanical ventilation onset.

Yes, aggressive polyvalent antivenin use for rattlesnake bites can result in serious acute side effects, but they appear uncommon: in a retrospective series, acute side effects occurred in 18% of treated patients, while only 2% had a serious reaction requiring intravenous epinephrine.
Among 65 patients who received antivenin (mean dose 12.0 ± 6.0 vials; 66% received ≥10 vials), acute side effects within 6 hours occurred in 12 patients (18%; 95% CI 10%-30%).

All but one of these reactions were urticaria; the single serious reaction occurred in a patient with a previous antivenin reaction who needed a short course of IV epinephrine for blood pressure support (2%; 95% CI 0%-8%), and no other complications occurred.
No.

In 87 patients with typical trigeminal neuralgia randomized to gamma knife radiosurgery (75 Gy maximal dose, 4-mm collimators), pain relief was identical whether one isocenter (n = 44) or two isocenters (n = 43) were used to increase nerve length within the treatment volume.
The actuarial complete pain relief rate was 67.7% ± 5.1%, and complete relief occurred in 57 patients, but it did not differ by isocenter number.

Instead, complications such as facial numbness or paresthesias correlated with the nerve length irradiated (p = 0.018), while improved pain relief correlated with younger age (p = 0.025) and fewer prior procedures (p = 0.039).
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether a specific patient has Crohn's disease.
In a retrospective study of 130 children suspected of IBD, the final diagnosis was Crohn's disease in 27, ulcerative colitis in 9, miscellaneous colitis in 13, and normal or probably normal in 81.

99mTc-WBC scans were positive in all but three newly diagnosed Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or miscellaneous colitis children, with false negatives seen in mild inflammation and normal UGI-SBFT.
Another study enrolled 49 patients already diagnosed with Crohn's disease to assess subclinical inflammation in relatives.
Thus, these passages describe diagnostic test performance and cohorts, not an individual diagnosis.

The evidence is mixed: delay in transfer to a rehabilitation unit for older patients with proximal femur fracture was associated with longer total hospital length of stay but did not predict discharge to a more dependent residence.
In an observational study of 455 patients aged over 75 years with proximal femur fracture, 58% were transferred to a rehabilitation ward.
Each day of delay in transfer was associated with a 0.64-day increase in total hospital length of stay (95% CI 0.23–1.05).
However, among transferred patients, only age over 85 years predicted discharge to a more dependent residence (relative risk 1.47, 95% CI 1.15–1.88), not delay in transfer.
The other supplied passage concerns proximal humerus fractures and does not address this question.
No—clinical variables did not accurately predict pathologic radiographs in the first episode of wheezing.
In a prospective convenience sample of children with a first episode of wheezing, pathologic radiographs were identified in 61 patients (9%).

Only pretreatment oxygen saturation differed significantly between the pathologic and nonpathologic groups; clinical score, respiratory rate, and presence of rales before or after treatment were not significantly different.
A discriminant analysis correctly predicted 90% of nonpathologic radiographs but only 15% of pathologic radiographs.
Yes—in a retrospective comparative cohort, hospice enrollment among dying nursing home residents with daily pain was associated with improved pain management.
The study compared 709 hospice and 1,326 nonhospice residents with daily pain near the end of life across over 800 nursing homes.

Hospice residents were less likely to receive no analgesics (15% vs 23%; OR=0.57, 95% CI=0.45-0.74) and less likely to receive analgesics not recommended by AMDA (21% vs 29%; OR=0.65, 95% CI=0.52-0.80).
They were also more likely to receive regular treatment for daily pain (51% vs 33%; adjusted OR=2.08, 95% CI=1.68-2.56).
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether rugby headgear prevents concussion.

One survey of 63 Canadian players (plus coaches from four levels) found that 62% of players believed headgear could prevent concussion versus 33% of coaches, but it assessed attitudes and wear, not whether headgear reduced concussions.

The other supplied studies examined pediatric emergency department concussion follow-up (ages 8-17) and bicycle-related injuries (1602 cases, 1540 controls; 141 concussions) and did not test rugby headgear; the bicyclist analysis found no association for concussion only.
Thus the passages do not show that rugby headgear does or does not prevent concussion.

The evidence is insufficient to establish that hepatitis G virus or TT virus are involved in cryptogenic chronic liver disease, because HGV and TTV markers were not significantly more frequent in cryptogenic disease than in HCV-related chronic liver disease.

In 23 patients with cryptogenic chronic liver disease versus 40 with HCV-related disease, HGV RNA was found in 4/23 (17.4%) versus 6/40 (15%, p=ns), any HGV marker in 6/23 (26.1%) versus 16/40 (40%, p=ns), and TTV-DNA in only 1 cryptogenic versus 2 HCV patients.
Demographic and clinical features, including liver histology, were comparable between HGV-infected and uninfected subjects, and severe liver damage was more frequent in HCV disease.
Other supplied passages note that the relevance of HGV/GBV-C in chronic hepatitis remains debated and that TTV status did not alter liver-specific biochemical parameters in hemodialysis patients.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether escalation of the apical dose changes treatment outcome in 106Ru plaque beta-radiation of posterior choroidal melanomas. The only relevant study treated 48 patients with posterior uveal melanomas (median height 3.85 mm plus 1 mm sclera) using ruthenium plaques at a median apical dose of 120 Gy and median scleral dose of 546 Gy, with 90% local control and 90% 5-year overall survival. Although its stated purpose included reviewing the optimal apical dose prescription (100 vs.
160 Gy), the supplied results do not compare outcomes between different apical dose levels.
Yes, a larger side-to-side systolic brachial blood pressure difference appears to be associated with more severe subclavian steal syndrome (SSS).

In a retrospective study of 49 patients with sonographically proven SSS (51 studies), systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in the complete reversal (31%) and alternating flow (47%) groups than in the systolic deceleration group (22%) (P<.001).

The study compared blood pressure difference (normal side minus lesion side) with three vertebral artery waveform types, but it does not establish the predictive accuracy of this difference for individual patients.
Yes, further investigation is warranted after a convulsion with retinal haemorrhage.

In a prospective study of 153 children aged 2 months to 2 years seen in the emergency department after a convulsive episode, one child had unilateral retinal haemorrhages following a simple febrile convulsion, and a thorough investigation uncovered no other reason for this finding.
Because retinal haemorrhages are considered characteristic of child abuse, this finding supports looking further to rule out systemic disorder or child abuse.
The prevalence of retinal haemorrhages after convulsions is not well established.
No, admission to a tertiary center with onsite coronary revascularization did not improve survival among elderly patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock.

In a Cooperative Cardiovascular Project analysis of 601 Medicare patients aged ≥65 with AMI complicated by cardiogenic shock, 287 (47.8%) were admitted to hospitals without revascularization services and 314 (52.2%) to hospitals with coronary angioplasty and CABG facilities.

Although patients at revascularization hospitals were more likely to undergo coronary revascularization during the index hospitalization and first month, after adjustment the presence of onsite revascularization services was not associated with significantly lower 30-day mortality (odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.47–1.45) or 1-year mortality (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.49–1.72).

No, the supplied evidence indicates these risk factors do not confer equal risk in women and men; in a direct sex-specific comparison, systolic blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking were stronger risk factors in women, and triglyceride risk was significantly higher in women.
In that comparison, fasting blood glucose ≥6.7 mmol/L carried a hazard ratio of 2.65 in women versus 2.08 in men, and smoking increased risk two- to five-fold in women versus a doubling in men.
Serum cholesterol was a significant risk factor in both sexes, but the passage does not report an equal sex-specific effect.

A separate meta-analysis also found significant heterogeneity across studies in relative risks for systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, smoking, and diabetes (p<0.05 for homogeneity), although it did not directly compare women with men.

No, postoperative antibiotics did not decrease post-tonsillectomy morbidity in a tonsillectomy audit that found they had no role in pain control, postoperative fever, secondary hemorrhage, or reduction in hospital stay.
The audit included 185 patients undergoing tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy (ages 2–53 years, mostly children) and did not provide numerical effect estimates for these outcomes.
The evidence is mixed: concentric leg muscle power was generally not related to running speed with changes of direction, while reactive strength showed some moderate significant correlations.

In 15 male participants with recent experience in sports involving sprints with changes of direction, 8 m sprints were timed straight and with various changes of direction, and leg extensor concentric power was tested via isokinetic squat and reactive strength via drop jump.
Correlations between concentric power and change-of-direction speed were generally low and non-significant, whereas some moderate significant (p<0.05) coefficients were found for reactive strength.
No, the evidence suggests routine pelvic CT is not necessary in renal cell carcinoma because all pelvic abnormalities found on CT were already detected by other investigations.

In 400 RCC patients (114 stage I, 68 stage II, 99 stage III, 119 stage IV), only 14 (3.5%) had a pelvic abnormality on CT, including 6 (1.5%) malignant, but all 14 were detected prior to CT by ultrasound or plain x-ray.
The other supplied passages do not address pelvic CT necessity in RCC.

Yes—a special interest in laparoscopy appears to affect treatment of acute cholecystitis: patients cared for by laparoscopic specialists had a higher rate of successful laparoscopic treatment. In a retrospective review of 170 acute cholecystitis patients, 48 were treated by three laparoscopic specialists and 122 by nine general surgeons who performed laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Successful laparoscopic treatment occurred in 65% of specialist patients vs 36% of general-surgeon patients (p=0.001), and median postoperative stay was shorter (3 vs 5 days, p<0.01). Postoperative complications were similar (31% vs 37%, p=0.6), and specialist group status predicted successful laparoscopic operation (p<0.01) but not prolonged length of stay after adjustment (p=0.21).
Yes—physiologic evidence indicates that mossy fibers release GABA.

In hippocampal slices from 3- to 5-week-old guinea pigs, electrical stimuli that recruit dentate granule cells elicited monosynaptic GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic signals in CA3 pyramidal neurons, and these signals met criteria for mossy fiber-CA3 synapses (metabotropic glutamate-receptor agonist sensitivity, facilitation during repetitive stimulation, and NMDA receptor-independent long-term potentiation).
Mossy fiber terminals also show intense GABA and GAD67 immunoreactivity, and the review's purpose was to present physiologic evidence of GABA release by mossy fibers.
Yes, lower fasting plasma glucose (FPG) at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is associated with improved outcomes, based on fewer diabetic complications and reduced risks in the UKPDS cohort.
Among 5,088 of 5,102 UKPDS participants, outcomes were compared by FPG at diagnosis: low (<140 mg/dl), intermediate (140 to <180 mg/dl), or high (>=180 mg/dl).
Fewer people in the lowest FPG category had retinopathy, abnormal biothesiometer measurements, or erectile dysfunction.

The low FPG group had significantly reduced risk for each predefined clinical outcome except stroke, and both low and intermediate groups had reduced risk for retinopathy progression, vibration threshold reduction, or microalbuminuria development.

The evidence is insufficient to establish increased neutrophil migratory activity after major trauma as a causal factor in the etiology of ARDS; the relevant study shows enhanced migration but does not directly link it to ARDS development.

In 17 adult blunt trauma patients with Injury Severity Score ≥18, neutrophils isolated at admission and 8 and 24 hours later migrated significantly more to interleukin-8 at 30 and 100 ng/mL than neutrophils from 9 normal volunteers (p<.05).

Neutrophil counts in whole blood were elevated at admission in patients who later developed ARDS and declined over 24 hours, but the migration results were not compared between patients who did and did not develop ARDS.
Thus, the study supports a plausible mechanism but does not prove that enhanced neutrophil migratory activity causes ARDS.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that withdrawal-induced anxiety in alcoholism is based on beta-endorphin deficiency, though beta-endorphin levels are lowered and inversely correlated with anxiety during withdrawal. In a consecutive sample of 60 alcoholics assessed on day 1 and day 14 after onset of withdrawal and 30 healthy volunteers, beta-endorphin was significantly lowered on both days relative to controls. Self-rated anxiety decreased significantly between day 1 and day 14, and beta-endorphin levels were inversely correlated with anxiety on day 1 (r=-0.58) and day 14 (r=-0.71), with partial correlations controlling for ACTH showing this was largely independent of ACTH. However, the study's objective was to test whether beta-endorphin is associated with anxiety, not to establish causation, so it does not prove that withdrawal-induced anxiety is based on beta-endorphin deficiency.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that HELLP syndrome is evidence of a possible systemic inflammatory response in pre-eclampsia, because the supplied passages did not measure systemic inflammation or inflammatory markers.
The passages define HELLP syndrome and compare outcomes such as neonatal morbidity, maternal platelet counts, and biochemical changes.

For example, one study compared HELLP syndrome, partial HELLP syndrome, and severe pre-eclampsia for neonatal outcome , and another found consanguinity had no effect on HELLP syndrome among pre-eclamptic women.
Therefore, they do not show whether HELLP syndrome reflects a systemic inflammatory response in pre-eclampsia.
Yes—anorectal endosonography appears valuable in dyschesia because it demonstrated dysfunction of the anal sphincter and/or m. puborectalis in patients with the condition.

In a prospective study of 20 dyschesia patients versus 20 healthy controls, the anal sphincter became paradoxically shorter and/or thicker during straining in 85% of patients versus 35% of controls (p<0.01), and the m. puborectalis did so in 80% versus 30% (p<0.01).
These significant differences indicate that endosonography can distinguish dyschesia patients from controls, supporting its value for this evaluation.
Yes—in high-risk metastatic breast cancer, first-line single-agent mitoxantrone was as effective as combination chemotherapy with FEC on efficacy outcomes.
In a randomized trial of 260 previously untreated women with measurable high-risk metastatic breast cancer, mitoxantrone 12 mg/m2 was compared with FEC every 3 weeks.

Single-agent mitoxantrone did not differ significantly from FEC in response, objective remission rate, remission duration, time to response, time to best response, time to progression, or overall survival, and no subgroup fared better with combination treatment; a modified Brunner's score for treatment gain favored single-agent mitoxantrone.

The evidence is mixed: prepuncture ultrasound facilitated right internal jugular vein cannulation in adults in whom respiratory jugular venodilation was not identified, but not in those in whom it was identified.
In a randomized study of 240 adults undergoing general anesthesia at a single community hospital, right IJV cannulation was attempted with either anatomic landmarks or prepuncture ultrasound.

Among the 188 patients (78.3%) with respiratory jugular venodilation, first-attempt access (83.5% landmark vs 85.7% ultrasound), success within 3 attempts (96.9% vs 95.6%), and arterial puncture (1.0% vs 3.3%) did not differ.
Among the remaining 52 patients without venodilation, ultrasound improved access (86.2% vs 30.4%, p<0.001) and success (100% vs 78.3%, p<0.05) and reduced arterial puncture (0% vs 13.0%).
The evidence is insufficient to say whether circumcision should be performed in childhood, because the supplied studies compare timing or alternatives rather than directly answering that question.

In a prospective cohort of 350 infants, complications including meatal deformities, meatal stenosis, adhesions and infection were more frequent and more significant in 250 neonates circumcised at 1 to 4 days than in 100 infants circumcised at 5 months.
Another study aimed to evaluate prepuce development and retractibility and the value of circumcision and forced dilation during childhood, but the supplied passage gives no outcome data.

Among 128 parents/children responding after preputioplasty, 108 (84%) were satisfied with function and 102 (80%) reported good cosmetic outcome, while 91 (71%) feared disadvantages in their son's later life if the child had been circumcised.
Yes—a written information sheet improved recall in patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty.

In a prospective randomized controlled study, 126 patients undergoing revision or primary total hip arthroplasty were assigned to written information with explanation (61 patients) or verbal information alone (65 patients).
Recall tested by questionnaire on admission (mean 18 days later) was significantly higher in the written group, with 48% correct answers versus 38% in the verbal group.
Yes, a randomized double-blind trial found that ibuprofen increased perioperative blood loss during total hip replacement.

In 50 patients pretreated for 2 weeks before surgery, the ibuprofen group had a 45% increase in perioperative blood loss compared with placebo, with total blood loss of 1161 ± 472 mL versus 796 ± 337 mL.
However, eight patients in the ibuprofen group and six in the placebo group terminated participation because of severe adverse effects.
The evidence is mixed: cardiology-involving care was associated with better survival than general medicine alone, but cardiology-only care was not significantly better than combined care.
In a retrospective VHA cohort of 11,661 patients discharged with a primary diagnosis of CHF, 1-year mortality was lowest in the MIXED group (19%) and highest in the no-GM/CARD group (29%).
After adjustment, compared with MIXED care, the risk of death was 1.26 (1.15-1.38) for GM-only and 1.48 (1.28-1.72) for no-GM/CARD, while CARD-only was 1.12 (0.94-1.34).

Thus, the data show a survival advantage for care involving cardiology plus general medicine over general medicine alone or no such follow-up, but they do not show that cardiology-only specialty care independently improves survival over combined care.
The evidence is mixed for long-term survival and insufficient for morbidity in gastric cancer patients after gastrectomy.
In a retrospective study, gastric cancer patients who underwent gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy were subgrouped by BMI <0.185 versus >0.210 and compared for morbidity and long-term survival.
Lower BMI was associated with longer mean survival in stage 2 (1667 vs.

Yes—environmental exposures appear important in primary systemic vasculitis, based on a case-control study that found significant associations with farming, occupational silica/solvent exposure, and allergy.

In 75 PSV cases versus 273 controls, farming in the index year was associated with PSV (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.2-4.6), Wegener's granulomatosis (2.7, 1.2-5.8), microscopic polyangiitis (6.3, 1.9-21.6), and pANCA (4.3, 1.5-12.7).

High occupational silica exposure in the index year was associated with PSV (3.0, 1.0-8.4), CSS (5.6, 1.3-23.5), and ANCA (4.9, 1.3-18.6), while high solvent exposure and drug allergy were also associated with PSV or subgroups.
The study found no other significant associations, so it supports environmental factors but is a case-control design and does not establish causation.
Yes, a case report describes spinal subdural hematoma (SSDH) following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) from a ruptured internal carotid aneurysm, a presentation never previously reported.

The patient was a 52-year-old woman who underwent craniotomy for the ruptured aneurysm and developed severe lower back and buttock pain on postoperative day 6; MRI showed a lumbosacral subdural hematoma.
She was treated conservatively, with the hematoma resolving completely by 15 weeks and no neurologic deficit at discharge 7 weeks later.
This single case supports SSDH as a possible sequela, but the supplied passages do not establish incidence or causality beyond that report.
No, tumor depth should not be included as an independent prognostic factor in soft tissue sarcoma once grade and size are accounted for.

In a population-based series of 490 adults with extremity or trunk wall soft tissue sarcoma, multivariate analysis showed no major prognostic effect of depth when grade and size were taken into account.
Although depth influenced prognosis in the subset of high-grade, large tumors, this was explained by the larger mean size of deep-seated tumors.
The other supplied passages do not report depth-specific multivariable results.
The evidence is mixed/insufficient to conclude that cell death in mesial temporal sclerosis is apoptotic.

In temporal lobe specimens from 15 drug-resistant epilepsy patients with MTS (6 women, 9 men; mean age 29±8 years), there was increased Bax expression and caspase-cleaved actin (fractin) in approximately 10% of neurons, but no DNA fragmentation by TUNEL and no typical apoptotic nuclear changes by Hoechst-33258 or hematoxylin counterstaining.
Thus, although some apoptotic markers were present, the study could not confirm apoptotic cell death.
The other supplied passages address breast cancer and gene therapy models, not MTS.

The evidence is mixed/conditional: a decision analysis found that withholding anticoagulation is generally preferred after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), but anticoagulation could be preferred for deep hemispheric ICH if thromboembolic stroke risk is particularly high.

In a Markov model of a 69-year-old man with prior ICH and new nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, withholding warfarin improved quality-adjusted life expectancy by 1.9 QALYs for prior lobar ICH and by 0.3 QALYs for prior deep hemispheric ICH.
In sensitivity analyses for deep ICH, anticoagulation could be preferred if the risk of thromboembolic stroke is particularly high.

Observational data show that ICH patients on anticoagulants had larger median hemorrhage volumes (64.7 vs 27.2 cm3) and 1.74 times higher 7-day mortality, though no relationship with functional outcome and no association between reversal and outcome.
Yes, socioeconomic status matters for quality of life in lung cancer patients at baseline, but not at three-month follow-up.

In a prospective study of 129 newly diagnosed lung cancer patients (82 with complete data), 57% were of lower socioeconomic status and had more health problems, less functioning, and more symptoms than affluent patients.
At baseline, significant differences were found for physical mobility (P=0.05), energy (P=0.01), role functioning (P=0.04), physical functioning (P=0.03), and breathlessness (P=0.02).
At follow-up, however, there were no significant differences between groups and no consistent pattern emerged.
Yes, a 9-month treatment appears sufficient in tuberculous enterocolitis based on a randomized trial showing no recurrence.

In that trial, 40 patients with tuberculous enterocolitis were randomized to 9 months (n=22) or 15 months (n=18); complete response was obtained in all patients in both groups, and no recurrence of active intestinal tuberculosis occurred during follow-up in either group.
The evidence is limited by the small sample size, and a separate retrospective study of extrapulmonary tuberculosis did not specifically assess 9-month therapy for intestinal disease.

Yes, in rats Nd:YAG laser-induced thermo therapy (LITT) opened the blood-brain barrier locoregionally and allowed paclitaxel to cross into brain tissue, supporting it as a possible concept for adjuvant glioma therapy.

The evidence comes from CD Fischer rats receiving LITT to the left forebrain; BBB disruption was shown by Evans blue and immunohistochemical extravasation of C3C, fibrinogen, and IgM, and HPLC demonstrated paclitaxel passage across the disrupted BBB.

The passages do not report a glioma model, tumor response, survival, or a control comparison, and no quantitative paclitaxel levels are provided, so they support feasibility but not clinical efficacy.

Yes, progression of valvar aortic stenosis can be predicted using the degree of valvar calcification and the initial aortic valve opening area, though the supplied passage does not quantify how accurate that prediction is.

In 169 men and 88 women with aortic stenosis (mean age 55.2 years at first and 63.4 years at second catheterization), the progression rate depended on valvar calcification score 0 to III and was exponentially correlated with initial AVA, while age, sex, and etiology did not significantly influence progression.
Surgery was probable in the following years when AVA fell below 0.75 cm2 with VC 0, 0.8 cm2 with VC I, 0.9 cm2 with VC II, or 1.0 cm2 with VC III.
Other supplied passages address aortic wall pathology, low-gradient severe AS measurement, and bioprosthesis outcomes, not prediction of valvar AS progression.
Yes, communication with terminally ill patients can be taught, based on a 2-day course that improved participants' self-assessed communication security and behavior.

In the first three courses, 31 participants showed growing sense of security across seven communication settings, with important increases for communicating cancer diagnoses with good or poor prognosis, recurrence, or far-progressive disease without curative approach.
Three months after the course, participants reported multiple changes indicating increased sensibility and professionalism in communication behavior.
However, these findings rely on self-assessment and perceived changes rather than objective skill measures, so they do not establish durable objective competence.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether early discharge with nurse home visits affects adequacy of newborn metabolic screening, because the supplied passages do not assess nurse home visits.

In one study of 3860 infants, early discharge at 24-47 hours versus traditional stay was associated with more initial inadequate filter-paper specimens (22.9% vs 14.3%, P<.0001), but a higher repeat rate when the initial specimen was inadequate (85.0% vs 75.3%, P=.002) and more adequate specimens within 9 days (98.8% vs 96.7%, P=.0005).
In South Australia, early discharge before 3 days, especially less than 1 day, was among factors associated with missed newborn screening (overall screening rate 97.8% in 1999).
The other supplied cohort study assessed maternal confidence and adequacy of obstetric care, not metabolic screening or nurse home visits.

The evidence is insufficient to say whether a practicing surgeon can reliably detect early lymphedema, because the supplied passages report detection criteria, risk modeling, and imaging rather than surgeon examination performance.

In 90 breast cancer patients, 39 lymphedema cases were identified by an academic trial; circumference criteria detected 37% of cases using a 10% increase at two sites, 49% using a 10% increase at any site, and 91% using a 5% increase at any site.
Another passage describes a nomogram for predicting clinical and subclinical lymphedema after axillary lymph node dissection, but it does not test surgeon detection reliability.
A third reports high-resolution MR lymphangiography detecting lymph nodes and vessels in three patients with lower-extremity lymphedema, again not surgeon detection.
No, the sequence of clamp application during open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair did not influence distal embolisation in the supplied evidence.

Although reports had suggested that preferential clamping of the distal vessel(s) before the proximal aorta might decrease emboli, a randomised study of 40 patients undergoing AAA repair found no difference between first clamping of the proximal aorta versus the iliac vessels in the number of emboli detected passing through the superficial femoral arteries (p=0.49).
That study also found no significant correlation between the number of emboli and dissection time (r=0.0008).
The evidence is mixed and does not show that double reading of barium enemas is necessary.

In 994 consecutive barium enemas, adding a second reader increased positive results from 249 to 315 (p<0.0001) and potentially altered clinical treatment in 98 patients (9.9%), but sensitivity for all lesions was identical at 76.3% and specificity decreased from 91.0% to 86.4%, with the second reading taking an average of 3.3 minutes.
The other supplied passages address follow-up after double-contrast barium enema and barium meals for pyloric stenosis, not double reading, so they do not resolve the question.
Yes—among prostate cancer patients who developed metastases after radiotherapy, those with ≤5 metastatic lesions had significantly better overall survival than those with >5 lesions.

In a retrospective cohort of 369 patients with Stage T1-T3aN0-NXM0 prostate cancer treated with curative-intent external beam radiotherapy (mean 65 Gy), 74 (20%) developed metastases, and the ≤5 lesion group had 5- and 10-year overall survival of 73% and 36% vs 45% and 18% for >5 lesions (p=0.02).

The same study reported superior metastasis-free survival and longer interval from diagnosis to bone metastasis for ≤5 lesions (p=0.01 and 0.02), but no significant difference in survival from bone metastasis diagnosis to death (p=0.17).

The other supplied passages did not report outcomes by oligometastatic status; one described metastatic site groups but provided no results , and the other addressed risk stratification after prostatectomy, not oligometastases.

Yes, survival appears to be improving, based on improved prognosis in women diagnosed with breast cancer before age 50 and longer survival in more recent recurrent-breast-cancer cohorts, though for recurrent/metastatic disease the adjusted improvement was only a trend. For patients diagnosed before age 50, cumulative 40-year relative survival is now approximately 43% for all cancers combined, 57% for localized cancers, and 24% for regional spread. Among 834 women who developed recurrent breast cancer between 1974 and 2000 after adjuvant anthracycline-based therapy, unadjusted survival improved across five groups by year of recurrence (P<0.001), and multivariate analysis showed a 1% reduction in risk for each increasing year.

No—for prognostic stratification, sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma was not clinically meaningful in a Danish population-based cohort of children aged 0–14 years: there was no survival difference between pilocytic and fibrillary astrocytoma, and the WHO and Kernohan systems had no predictive value (Daumas-Duport was unsuitable).

That study followed patients from 1960–1984 to 2001, with an overall survival of 81% at 15–40 years, and found gross-total resection and cerebellar-proper location as the significant positive prognostic factors.
A separate series of 28 cerebellar low-grade gliomas reported outcomes (25/28 alive at median 112 months) but did not compare outcomes by subtype.

Another series of 174 CNS tumors found 30% diagnostic discordance in low-grade gliomas (10 upgraded to anaplastic astrocytoma, 10 no tumor) and histology changed management in 11 cases (10%) overall, but this was not specific to cerebellar astrocytoma sub-classification.

Yes, pain is a clinically relevant problem in general adult psychiatry, based on high prevalence and associated impairment/unfitness for work among psychiatric inpatients. In a cross-sectional questionnaire study of 106 patients primarily diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder in general adult psychiatry, point prevalence of pain was about 50%, 6-month prevalence 75.5%, and 12-month prevalence 76.5%. Almost 10% reported pain lasting at least 3 months in the past year, and impairment and unfitness for work were related to specific psychiatric diagnosis, with significant risk factors including depression (OR=6.05) and number of past psychiatric admissions (OR=3.609).
Yes, CT can help predict the level of CSF block in tuberculous hydrocephalus, but only through one finding: the shape of the third ventricle.

In a study of 50 children with communicating and 34 with non-communicating hydrocephalus confirmed by air-encephalography, the only CT index that correlated with the type of hydrocephalus was third-ventricle shape.
Significantly more children with non-communicating hydrocephalus had a rounded third ventricle than those with communicating hydrocephalus.
The passages do not show that other CT indices or a broader CT model can reliably predict the block level.
Yes—fear of anaphylaxis and/or dissemination appears to discourage surgeons from adopting percutaneous and laparoscopic techniques for liver hydatid cyst.
In a survey of 30 surgeons in northern Jordan, only 3 (10%) considered laparoscopy as first-line treatment.
Of the 27 surgeons who did not consider percutaneous or laparoscopic treatment, fear of anaphylaxis and/or dissemination was the main reason given by 21 (78%) for not using minimal-access techniques.
The evidence is limited to this single survey and does not establish broader generalizability.

Yes—among women treated with radiotherapy for Hodgkin's disease, treatment around the time of pregnancy was associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. In 382 women, the overall incidence was 16.0% in the pregnancy-associated group versus 2.3% in nonpregnant women (p=0.0001), and 10- and 15-year actuarial rates were 6.7% and 32.6% versus 0.4% and 1.7% (p=0.011). Multivariate analysis found pregnancy around radiotherapy was the only associated variable, with a hazard ratio of 22.49 (95% CI 5.56-90.88; p<0.001) for radiotherapy during pregnancy or within 1 month of pregnancy compared with nonpregnant women and those irradiated later than 1 month after pregnancy.
No, the one direct test found no significant gender differences in self-report of depression symptoms, suggesting differential symptom reporting does not account for higher depression rates in women.

In a population-based 13-year follow-up of 1,727 community-dwelling adults in East Baltimore, women were no more likely than men to endorse sadness after adjustment for age, ethnicity, education, marital status, and employment (adjusted direct effect 0.105, 95% CI -0.113 to 0.323).

Other passages confirm higher reported rates of depression and anxiety in women and show higher depression rates for females only in some alcohol-use-disorder symptom patterns , but they do not directly test differential symptom reporting.
Thus the evidence suggests the higher rates are not accounted for by differential symptom reporting, though this conclusion rests mainly on the single direct study.
No, acute heart rate changes induced by isoproterenol did not significantly affect aortic stiffness in patients with hypertension.
In 17 hypertensive patients (mean age 59 ± 9 years), pulse wave velocity, compliance, and compliance index were measured as percent changes from baseline during graded isoproterenol infusion.
There were no significant group differences in deltaPWV, deltaC, or deltaCi (p>0.05), and deltaHR did not correlate significantly with deltaPWV or deltaC (r=0.18 and 0.13, p>0.05).
Although deltaCi showed a weak correlation with deltaHR (r=0.22, p<0.05), only 4.6% of its variation was explained by heart rate change.
The supplied passages do not settle whether peer review has a role in profiling quality of care, because none directly tests that question.

PMID:15151701 evaluated a structured implicit physician review instrument for quality of care in 70 patient records with 496 reviews, finding single-reviewer reliability (intra-class correlation) of 0.16–0.26 for COPD/acute conditions and 0.46 for diabetes/hypertension.
PMID:23920433 notes that profiling is used for improvement and requires an appropriate statistical model to reflect true provider performance, but it does not address peer review.
PMID:22350231 compares traditional peer review of manuscripts with post-publication reader review in a computer model, which is not about profiling quality of care.
No—patients with diabetes are not receiving entirely the same message from dietitians and nurses, based on a survey of certified diabetes educators.
Among 366 CDEs (207 RNs and 159 RDs) in the southern United States, no statistically significant differences were found between RNs and RDs in typical carbohydrate recommendations for diabetes.

However, RDs were more likely than RNs to recommend fiber intake or use of the glycemic index, and RNs were more likely than RDs to recommend consuming a carbohydrate source with protein to treat hypoglycemia.
Yes, the Omega-3 Index is supported as a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease (CHD).

In the relevant study, the Omega-3 Index (red blood cell EPA + DHA) was inversely associated with risk for CHD mortality, with an index ≥8% associated with the greatest cardioprotection and ≤4% with the least.
This rests on evidence that low EPA + DHA intake or blood levels are independently associated with increased CHD death risk and that RBC fatty acid composition reflects long-term intake.
The relationship was evaluated in published primary and secondary prevention studies.

Yes, preclinical evidence supports c-Kit-dependent growth in uveal melanoma and identifies it as a potential therapeutic target, based on a study showing c-kit expression, phosphorylation, and sensitivity to the c-kit inhibitor STI571.

In that study, c-kit was expressed in 84 of 134 paraffin-embedded uveal melanoma specimens and 6 of 8 fresh-frozen samples, and was strongly expressed and tyrosine-phosphorylated in three uveal melanoma cell lines (OCM-1, OCM-3, 92-1) compared with cutaneous melanoma cells.

The same cell lines produced the c-kit ligand (stem cell growth factor), suggesting autocrine/paracrine stimulation, and treatment with STI571 blocked c-kit autophosphorylation and caused cell death with an IC50 <2.5 microM for both phosphorylation and proliferation.

No, sports medicine journals appear not to be highly relevant or applicable to everyday practice for practitioners and athletes, based on an analysis of four major sport and exercise medicine journals.

Most published articles focused on sports science, with very few studies on treatment of injuries or medical conditions, and the majority used healthy subjects from the sedentary population rather than injured participants.

Other supplied passages do not directly address this question, as they studied general sports medicine texts , compared material in medical journals for general practitioners , and compared coding of sports medicine diagnoses.
Yes, the type of remission after a major depressive episode is an important risk factor for relapse over a 4-year follow-up.

In a naturalistic study of 139 Spanish outpatients with DSM-III-R unipolar major depressive episode followed monthly for more than 4 years, the relapse rate was 91.4% in the partial remission group compared with 51.3% in the complete remission group.
Partial remission versus complete remission was one of four predictive factors, and partial remission was the most powerful predictive factor for relapse.
The evidence is mixed or insufficient to say that a general 'early adopter of drugs' exists.

Among 308 customers in two south London gay dance clubs, club-goers were considered 'early adopters' of psychostimulant/club drug trends, and mephedrone supplemented rather than replaced established club drugs.

However, in general practitioners, adoption of one drug group was poorly associated with adoption of others (r ≤ 0.49), indicating that early adoption of one type of drug is not associated with early adoption of another.
Thus the passages show an early-adopter label in a specific club-drug population but do not support a general, cross-drug early-adopter trait.

The evidence is mixed: an exploratory meta-analysis of two randomized controlled trials in stroke patients found a definite relationship between maximum reduction in arm spasticity and maximum improvement in arm function, independent of treatment, but the relationship was clear only for certain botulinum toxin doses.

In 137 patients, the correlation between maximum change in spasticity and maximum change in arm function was rho = -0.2822 (p = 0.0008); for botulinum toxin (Dysport) at 500 units it was rho = -0.5679 (p = 0.0090, n = 22) and at 1000 units rho = -0.4430 (p = 0.0018, n = 47), but no significant relationship was seen with placebo or 1500 units.
Maximum changes in spasticity and function occurred concurrently in 47 patients, with spasticity improvement preceding functional improvement in 26 and the reverse in 18.

Yes, expert breast pathology assessment appears necessary for DCIS management based on a study showing that secondary expert review changed local recurrence risk assessment in 29% and treatment recommendations in 43% of cases. In 350 patients with DCIS referred to a single regional cancer centre (1982–2000), inter-observer agreement was high for main pathologic features, but from 1996 to 2000, secondary pathology assessments changed risk assessment in 100 cases (29%) and contributed to a change in treatment recommendation in 93 (43%) cases. Another supplied study set out to determine whether mandatory pathology review changes diagnosis or surgical management of breast disease, but its results are not provided in the passages.
Yes.

They also had lower biochemical failure (12% versus 20%, P=0.01), improved biochemical disease-free survival especially for Gleason sum 7 or greater (P<0.01), and lower odds of biochemical failure (OR 0.57, P<0.001) compared with 1115 patients with no prior biopsy.
Thus, prior benign prostate biopsy predicts more favorable outcomes in this surgical population.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that combining 2-methoxyestradiol with chemotherapy can reduce chemotherapeutic dosages in human ovarian cancer treatment.

In two human ovarian cancer cell lines, 2ME (0.8-25 microM) combined with epirubicine, doxorubicine, paclitaxel, docetaxel, carboplatin, vinorelbine, 5-fluorouracil, or mafosfamide produced a significant additive antiproliferative effect only with epirubicine and carboplatin, at the lower concentration range of those chemotherapeutics.
This in vitro finding suggests a possible dose-sparing effect but does not show that dosages can be reduced in patients.

No, increased private health care use was not associated with reduced NHS demand in a UK study; NHS referral rates were significantly higher (rate ratio 1.40, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.71, p=0.001) in wards with private referral rates in the top fifth compared with the bottom fifth after adjustment for deprivation and practice.

The study included 17,137 referrals from 10 general practices, with 90.4% to the NHS and 9.6% to the private sector, and private referral rates were lower in deprived areas (rate ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.41).

This is an observational association and cannot establish causation; the remaining passages concern disease prevention, rheumatoid arthritis care, and managed care penetration, and do not address the relationship between private care and NHS demand.
The evidence is indirect but suggests yes: regions with predominantly inhaled steroid use had lower asthma hospital admission rates than a region with more cromone use.

Among children aged 6 years or older, total admissions were 0.3/1000 in Oulu vs 1.2/1000 in Kuopio, first admissions 0.2/1000 vs 1.0/1000, readmissions 6.3% vs 19.3%, and hospital days 0.7/1000 vs 3.8/1000, all favoring Oulu.

However, this is an ecological comparison of provinces and does not directly compare individual children treated with inhaled steroids versus cromones, so it cannot definitively establish a difference.

Yes, socioeconomic status matters for postpartum learning needs: in a Canadian survey, women of low socioeconomic status were significantly more likely to report unmet learning needs on 9 of 10 topics than women of higher socioeconomic status.

Among 45 resected stage III patients, 38 received radiation and baseline prognostic factors were similar; adjuvant radiotherapy did not alter local or distant recurrence rates.
Ten-year disease-specific survival was 79% with radiation versus 75% without (p = 0.21).
This small retrospective series suggests radiation may not be necessary, though wide confidence intervals and its design limit definitive conclusions.
Yes—some U.S. states appear to have higher or lower injury mortality rates than others, based on a study of states with the highest and lowest road traffic death rates.
That study compared the six U.S. states with the highest road traffic death rates (group 1) and the six with the lowest (group 2) from 1983 to 1995 across 13 injury categories.
Seventy-four percent of group 1 states had above-average rates of other injuries, and 85% of group 2 states conformed to the converse hypothesis.
The passage does not show all injury causes or all states, but it does show state-level variation for road traffic deaths and several other injury types.
Yes—serum pancreatic lipase should replace serum amylase as the primary biomarker for acute pancreatitis because it had better diagnostic accuracy in a large emergency department cohort.

In 8,937 emergency department patients (from 10,931 total patients and 17,531 measurements), ROC analysis showed an AUC of 0.948 for lipase versus 0.906 for amylase (P<0.05), and at the diagnostic threshold lipase had 90.3% sensitivity versus 76.8% for amylase, with similar specificity (93% vs 92.6%).
Only 2.9% of acute pancreatitis patients lacked elevated lipase versus 18.8% lacking elevated amylase on the first emergency department measurement.
In hypertriglyceridemic and lithiasic acute pancreatitis, lipase also supported the diagnosis more often than amylase (58% vs 26% and 79% vs 58%, respectively).
Yes—the evidence supports a potential role for uterine natural killer cells in irregular endometrial bleeding among menopausal hormone therapy users.

In a prospective study of 117 postmenopausal women taking combined HT, endometrial CD56+ uNK cells were significantly increased in biopsies obtained during bleeding episodes compared with HT users with no bleeding (P<0.001), and the highest IL-15 expression was also seen in biopsies taken during bleeding.
No clear relationship between killer Ig-like receptor genotype and bleeding on HT was observed.
Yes, the evidence indicates grandmultiparity is an independent risk factor for several adverse perinatal outcomes.

In a California study of 25,512 grandmultiparous women and 265,060 multiparous women aged 30 years or older with singleton deliveries, after controlling for potential confounders, grandmultiparous women had significantly higher risks of abruptio placentae (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2-1.5), preterm delivery (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2-1.4), fetal macrosomia (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.4-1.6), neonatal death (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3-1.8), postpartum hemorrhage (OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.1-1.3), and blood transfusion (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3-1.8).
Other supplied passages address different risk factors or methods and do not directly assess grandmultiparity as an independent risk factor.
Yes—limited evidence from one cross-sectional study links fast food to asthma symptoms in children.

In 1321 children (mean age 11.4 years) in New Zealand, after adjustment for lifestyle, diet, and BMI, hamburger consumption was independently associated with a history of wheeze (OR 1.44 for <1/week, 1.65 for ≥1/week) and current wheeze (OR 1.17 for <1/week, 1.81 for ≥1/week), while takeaway consumption ≥1/week was marginally associated with bronchial hyperresponsiveness (OR 2.41, 95% CI 0.99–5.91).
There was no effect on atopy.
Other supplied passages did not examine fast food; they reported associations of asthma with smoking, breastfeeding, fruit/vegetable intake, air pollution, and socioeconomic factors.
No—bedside assessment does not reliably exclude aspiration after acute stroke, because it missed half of patients who were aspirating on videofluoroscopy.
Among 94 consecutive patients admitted within 24 h of stroke onset, 20 (21%) aspirated on videofluoroscopy, but bedside assessment did not detect aspiration in 10 of them.

Yes, correlated results are possible from homebrew BCRABL quantitative real-time PCR assays, based on a two-laboratory comparison that found a strong correlation despite different assay components.

In 70 clinical specimens tested at Vanderbilt and Virginia Commonwealth, 43 were negative at both sites and 22 yielded paired BCRABL-positive results across a dynamic range of 10^0 to 10^5 per 100,000 cells.
Although RNA isolation, cDNA synthesis, BCR control cell line, and primer/probe sequences differed, the Spearman rank correlation for the 22 positive pairs was r_s=0.9435 (p<0.00001).
One discordant result occurred in consecutive samples from a patient with low BCRABL copy number due to minimal RNA yield at one laboratory.
The evidence indicates that differences between Landolt C and Snellen E acuity in strabismus amblyopia are small, with Snellen E slightly higher.

In a study of 100 patients (including 39 with strabismus amblyopia) and 13 healthy volunteers, the mean decimal acuity for the strabismus amblyopia eyes was 0.14 with Landolt C and 0.16 with Snellen E.

Yes, end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) measurement correlated with arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2) in ventilated extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infants in the first week of life.
In a retrospective study of 31 ELBW infants (<1,000 g), there were 754 paired EtCO2 and arterial CO2 measurements, and the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.81.
EtCO2 was significantly lower than PaCO2, with an overall bias of 5.6 +/- 6.9 mmHg, and EtCO2 exceeded PaCO2 in only 89/754 (11.8%) pairs.
Using EtCO2 ranges of 30 to 50 mmHg, capnography identified 84% of instances where PaCO2 was between 35 and 55 mmHg.
The evidence is mixed: in 125 peripheral PTA procedures, hydrophilic guidewires significantly improved technical success for SFA stenosis and iliac and SFA occlusions but not for iliac stenosis.

The study defined technical success as lesion crossing by guidewire and balloon, dilation with <30% residual stenosis, and ABI rise ≥0.15 at 24 hours.

Complete in-hospital continuity (preoperative and postoperative assessment) was 57%, and emergent cases had higher preoperative assessment (92% vs 63%, P<.05).

Yes, obstructive sleep apnea severity predicts the need for high continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), with severe OSA patients having a 5.90-fold higher frequency of high CPAP use after adjustment.
In 353 OSA patients who had successful manual CPAP titration, mean optimal CPAP increased from 7.79 cm H2O in mild to 8.7 in moderate to 10.1 in severe OSA.
High CPAP (≥12 cm H2O) was required by 2 (6.9%) mild, 6 (5.8%) moderate, and 63 (28.6%) severe OSA patients.
Yes, pancreatic-juice interleukin-8 concentration discriminated the presence of pancreatic disease, though the other measured cytokines did not.

In 118 patients with abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin who underwent secretin-stimulated endoscopic collection of pancreatic juice, multivariate analysis showed that only interleukin-8 discriminated normal pancreas from chronic pancreatitis (P =.011), pancreatic cancer (P =.044), and the presence of pancreatic diseases (P =.007).
Individual cytokine concentrations were not significantly different between chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer.
Thus the evidence supports predictive value specifically for interleukin-8 in pancreatic juice, not for all cytokine concentrations measured.

Bottom line: yes, preoperative tracheobronchoscopy matters in newborns with esophageal atresia because it was clinically useful in 45.2% and crucially modified the surgical approach in 24.2% of patients.

In a series of 62 newborns with EA who underwent preoperative flexible tracheobronchoscopy while breathing spontaneously, TBS identified unsuspected proximal fistula in 3 of 9 type A patients, previously undetected respiratory tree malformations in 4 patients, and allowed Fogarty catheter occlusion of carinal fistulas in 14 type C patients.
Overall, TBS was clinically useful in 28/62 (45.2%) and crucial in modifying the surgical approach in 15/62 (24.2%), with no complications observed.

Yes, by years 2 through 4, prefilled textured saline breast implants had significantly higher cumulative deflation rates than standard textured saline implants, although the year-1 difference was not significant. The evidence is insufficient to say whether histological features influence clinical presentation or outcome in pituitary apoplexy.

A retrospective analysis of 59 patients compared 22 with infarction alone versus 37 with hemorrhagic infarction and/or frank hemorrhage, assessing presenting symptoms, clinical features, endocrinological status, and outcome, but the supplied passages report only the objective and methods, not the comparative results.
The other supplied passages concern breast cancer, prostate cancer, and adenoid vegetation and are not relevant.

No, routine chest radiography after transbronchial biopsy does not appear necessary based on a study of 350 consecutive patients.

In that study, pneumothorax was diagnosed radiologically in 10 patients (2.9%); 7 had symptoms strongly suggestive of pneumothorax before CXR, including 4 with large >10% pneumothorax, while the other 3 were asymptomatic with only minimal <=10% pneumothorax that resolved completely in 24 to 48 h.
