The evidence is mixed and group-dependent: in a French study, breaching confidentiality to protect a wife from a patient's sexually transmitted disease was rated more acceptable by lay people and psychologists than by physicians (mean ratings 11.76, 9.28, and 2.90, respectively, on a 0-22 scale).

The study included 144 lay people, 10 psychologists, and 7 physicians judging 48 scenarios, and found the patient's stated intentions to protect and inform his wife had the greatest impact on acceptability.
Lay participants were not uniform: 14 found it always acceptable, 87 said it depended on many circumstances, 30 required consultation with an expert, and 13 found it never acceptable.
Thus the passages show qualified acceptability, especially among lay people and psychologists, but low acceptability among physicians and substantial variation by circumstances.
No, decisional algorithms cannot replace global introspection in the individual causality assessment of spontaneously reported ADRs, because they had low specificity despite high sensitivity.
In 500 adverse reports, an expert panel assessed causality using WHO global introspection while the same reports were independently assessed with 15 published algorithms.
The algorithms averaged 93% sensitivity and 89% positive predictive value but only 7% specificity and 31% negative predictive value.
This indicates they would misclassify many non-drug-related reports as drug related, so they are not a replacement for global introspection in individual assessment.
No—in this study of advanced NSCLC, cytostatic treatment was independently associated with better survival, so the skepticism is not supported.
The cohort included 190 patients with stage IV or IIIB NSCLC (pleural or N2–N3 involvement) and ECOG ≤2: 144 received cytostatic treatment and 46 received palliative treatment.

Median survival was 31 weeks, and cytostatic treatment had a hazard ratio of 1.85 (95% CI, 1.25–2.76; P=.002); among ECOG 2 patients, survival was 15 weeks with cytostatic treatment versus 11 weeks with symptomatic treatment.
The evidence is mixed: uterine myomas do not uniformly grow during pregnancy, and many decrease in volume.

In 107 pregnant patients with myomas who had two or more ultrasounds, between the first half of pregnancy and 20–30 weeks, 55.1% decreased in size (mean decrease 35%±4%) while 44.9% enlarged (mean increase 69%±11%).
Between 20–30 weeks and 31 weeks to term, 75% became smaller (mean decrease 30%±3%) while 25% enlarged (mean increase 102%±62%).
Thus, growth occurs in a substantial minority, but shrinkage is common, especially later in pregnancy.
Yes—at least specific self-reported health-related quality of life (HRQOL) domains are independent prognostic factors for survival in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

In 391 advanced NSCLC patients, pretreatment HRQOL measured with EORTC QLQ-C30/QLQ-LC13 was analyzed by multivariate Cox regression, which retained self-reported pain (HR 1.11, 95% CI 1.07–1.16; P<0.001) and dysphagia (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.04–1.21; P=0.003) as independent prognostic factors.

A 10-point worse score in pain or dysphagia was associated with an 11% and 12% increased likelihood of death, respectively, though this does not show that every HRQOL domain or changes during treatment predict survival.

No—supervised colorectal trainees did not differ significantly from consultants in the quality of TME surgery in the one supplied study addressing this, with good mesorectum in 41.5% of trainee operations versus 49% of consultant operations (P=0.717).

This study included 130 consecutive patients undergoing potentially curative resection for primary rectal adenocarcinoma from 2001–2003, comparing 89 consultant-performed operations with 41 operations by senior colorectal trainees under consultant supervision.
Local recurrence also did not differ significantly (9.5% trainee vs 7.8% consultant, P=0.719).

Yes, complex coronary lesions were more frequent in patients with diabetes mellitus, based on a study of 1014 consecutive patients undergoing coronary angiography in which bifurcation and ostial lesions were significantly more prevalent in the 281 diabetic patients than in the 733 nondiabetic patients.
Bifurcation lesions occurred in 9.8% of diabetics versus 4.3% of nondiabetics (P=0.001), and ostial lesions in 38.4% versus 29.2% (P=0.003).
Diabetes mellitus was also an independent predictor of both bifurcation lesions (OR=2.27, P=0.004) and ostial lesions (OR=1.40, P=0.027) in multivariate analysis.
The evidence specifically defines complex coronary lesions as bifurcation and ostial lesions in this study.

No, folic acid did not protect against congenital heart defects in Down syndrome; in a case-control study, first-trimester folic acid use showed no protective effect on heart anomalies overall (adjusted OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.61-1.47).

The analysis included women with liveborn Down syndrome children from the Slone Epidemiology Center Birth Defects Study (1976-1997), comparing 223 Down syndrome cases with heart anomalies to 184 Down syndrome controls without heart anomalies.
Exposure was any folic acid-containing product used at least 4 days per week during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, with 49% of cases exposed versus 46% of controls.
No protective effect was found separately for conotruncal defects, ventricular septal defects, ostium secundum atrial septal defects, or endocardial cushion defects.

No, frozen section did not alter surgical management in multinodular thyroid disease; in a retrospective series of 236 patients with multinodular goiter, none of the 135 who had intraoperative frozen section had their intraoperative management changed.
The sensitivity of frozen section for thyroid cancer in that group was only 25%, with three of four cancers misread as benign.
The other supplied studies address follicular lesions or papillary thyroid cancer neck dissection rather than multinodular disease, so they do not provide additional evidence on this question.
No, endoaortic balloon occlusion was not shown to be safe in this setting; it was associated with significantly higher in-hospital mortality.

In 52 of 2,172 consecutive patients selected for endoaortic occlusion because of aortic calcifications or epiaortic ultrasound findings, 10 (19.2%) required conversion to conventional cross-clamping for incomplete occlusion, hindered exposure, or balloon rupture.

In-hospital death occurred in 13 patients (25%) versus 4.2% in all other patients (p<0.0001), and multivariable analysis found endoaortic occlusion independently associated with death (OR 5.609, 95% CI 2.684–11.719); stroke was 3.8% versus 0.8% (p=0.067).

Evidence is mixed: in a retrospective cohort of 247 patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), overall maximum oxygen consumption (VO2max) was increased compared with normative data from 1.4 million US Air Force tests (p<.001), but patients with an apnea-hypopnea index greater than 20 had decreased VO2max compared with normalized values (p<.001).
No differences in VO2max were observed after medical or surgical therapy for OSA.

Thus, OSA may affect aerobic fitness in a severity-dependent direction, with overall higher VO2max but lower VO2max in more severe OSA; the other supplied passages do not report aerobic fitness outcomes.

No, fluoroscopy is not essential for retrieval of lower ureteric stones in most cases, as fluoro-less ureteroscopy achieved complete clearance in 99 of 110 patients (94.2%) with lower ureteral calculi.
In that study, fluoroscopy was required in only 6 patients (4%) for specific indications such as calcified stricture, duplex system, or difficult meatus.
A separate mixed cohort of 93 ureteral stones (52 distal, 30 middle, 11 proximal) had a 96.77% stone-free rate with fluoro-less endoscopic treatment, with fluoroscopy needed in 7 patients.
Another study reported a 93.3% stone-free rate for lower ureteric stones after ureteroscopic lithotripsy but did not assess fluoroscopy use.
Thus, fluoroscopy is not routinely essential but may be necessary in select cases.

The evidence is mixed: overall long-term post-pull-through scores were similar between transanal endorectal pull-through (TERPT) and transabdominal (ABD) pull-through, but continence was significantly better after ABD while stool pattern was better after TERPT.
This rests on 41 Hirschsprung disease patients older than 3 years (TERPT n = 20; ABD n = 21) assessed with a 15-item long-term outcome questionnaire.
A between-group age difference was present, but reanalysis controlling for age showed age did not significantly affect long-term scoring outcomes between groups.
Yes, the evidence supports a link between genetic and environmental factors in atrial fibrillation (AF) pathogenesis, based on a stretch-sensitive KCNQ1 mutation.

In mutation screening of 50 families with AF, one missense KCNQ1 mutation (R14C) was identified in a family with high hypertension prevalence, and AF occurred only in older genotype-positive individuals who had developed atrial dilation.

Patch-clamp studies of wild-type versus R14C channels showed no significant differences at baseline or after forskolin, but after hypotonic swelling to elicit stretch, mutant channels had a marked increase in current, a leftward shift in voltage dependence of activation, altered kinetics, and shortening of modeled atrial action potential duration.

No clear need for neck dissection is demonstrated in patients with metastatic carcinoma to cervical nodes from an unknown head and neck primary, because adding neck dissection to radiotherapy did not significantly improve outcomes.
In a series of 61 such patients, 41 had biopsy only and 20 underwent neck dissection, while all received radiotherapy.
The 8-year overall survival was 64.8% for biopsy vs 67.6% for neck dissection (p =.64), and local relapse-free survival was 75% vs 74.5% (p =.57).
This suggests neck dissection may be unnecessary in this setting, though the study is a single series and does not prove equivalence or rule out benefit in subsets.
Yes, size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement is an option in modern aortic surgery, though indications are not fully established.

In a retrospective series of 531 patients with ascending aortic aneurysm or ectasia (45–76 mm), 50 underwent size-reducing aortoplasty with external non-coated Dacron reinforcement, with 2% hospital mortality and significant diameter reduction (CT 55.8±9 to 40.51±6.2 mm, p<0.002; echocardiography 54.1±6.7 to 38.7±7.1 mm, p<0.002) that remained stable at mean 70-month follow-up.

A separate series of 81 adults with conotruncal anomalies included 9 combined aortic valve replacement and reduction aortoplasty, with no ascending aortic reoperations after prior reduction aortoplasty and no late aortic dissections over a median 3.8 years.
However, indications regarding aortic diameter, history of dilatation, and intraoperative management (wall excision, reduction suture, external reinforcement) are not established.
Bottom line: the evidence suggests bile duct sludge is not clearly different from bile duct stones in recurrence after endoscopic clearance, although some associated features differ.
In 228 patients undergoing therapeutic ERCP for suspected choledocholithiasis, bile duct sludge without stones occurred in 14% (31/228) and was more common in females.

After endoscopic clearance, recurrent CBD stones occurred in 16% (5/31) of patients with bile duct sludge versus 17% (33/197) of patients with CBD stones (p = 0.99), and other risk factors were not statistically different.
However, common bile duct dilation was less common in the sludge group.

The evidence is insufficient to answer whether ambulatory process of care predicts health-related quality of life outcomes in patients with chronic disease.

A separate analysis of adults with chronic disease characterized 347,606 patients and 7,662,411 ambulatory visits and examined access patterns, not HRQOL outcomes.
Other supplied passages link primary care quality to emergency department costs or compare QOL by treatment setting, but they do not test ambulatory process of care as a predictor of HRQOL.

Yes, renal warm ischemia over 30 minutes during laparoscopic partial nephrectomy is possible; 18 patients underwent LPN with warm ischemia time >30 min and at 1 year kidney damage markers and renal function showed complete return to the normal range with no statistical difference across time points.

In that series, GFR was not significantly different before and 3 months after surgery, and scintigraphy of the operated kidney was 48.35+/-3.82% before, 36.88+/-8.42% on postoperative day 5 (p=0.0001), 40.56+/-8.96% at 3 months (p=0.003), and 42.8+/-7.2% at 1 year (p=0.001), indicating partial recovery but a persistent reduction.

The remaining passages do not directly address LPN with >30 min warm ischemia: a rat study used 25 minutes of ischemia , and laparoscopic donor nephrectomy studies reported much shorter warm ischemia times.

The evidence is mixed: a 30-second antismoking advertisement shown before a movie improved non-smokers' perception that smoking in the movie was not OK (47.8% vs 43.8%, p=0.04) but had no significant effect on smokers' perception (16.5% vs 14.5%, p=0.4).

Among 3091 cinema patrons aged 12-24 in Australia, smokers who saw the advertisement were more likely to intend to smoke in 12 months (38.6% vs 25.6%, p<0.001), while non-smokers' intentions did not differ significantly (1.2% vs 1.6%, p=0.54).
Thus, the advertisement affected young people's perceptions and intentions in opposite directions depending on smoking status.
Yes, breast cancer prognosis appears to be inherited.

In a Swedish population-based cohort of 2,787 mother-daughter pairs and 831 sister pairs with breast cancer diagnosed from 1961 to 2001, daughters and sisters of a proband with poor 5-year prognosis had a 60% higher 5-year breast cancer mortality than those of a proband with good prognosis (HR, 1.6; 95% CI, 1.2-2.2; p for trend 0.002).
Five-year survival was 87% versus 91% for daughters depending on maternal outcome, and 70% versus 88% for sisters.
The other supplied passages concern pancreatic cancer predisposition or secular breast cancer prognosis, not inherited breast cancer prognosis.
Thus, the evidence supports inherited breast cancer prognosis, though it rests on this single cohort.
Yes, shaving the incision site before spinal surgery increased the postoperative infection rate in a prospective randomized clinical study.

Among 789 patients scheduled for spinal surgery, those randomized to shaving immediately before surgery (371 patients) had 4 postoperative infections, compared with 1 infection among 418 patients who were not shaved (P<0.01).
The study was specifically designed to determine whether shaving the incision site before spinal surgery causes postsurgical infection.

A separate background passage on spinal osteotomy notes that surgical site infection occurs in 0.7% to 12% of patients and that blood loss and surgical time are risk factors, but it does not address shaving.
Yes, there are gender differences in the factors associated with delay, although overall median delay time did not differ significantly.

The evidence is mixed: working in a rural location did not affect overall self-reported competence among midwives, but it was associated with differences in specific competencies.

However, rural midwives were more likely to report competence for breech delivery (p=0.001), while urban midwives more often reported competence in intravenous fluid replacement and initial/discharge newborn examination (both p<0.001).
The evidence is mixed: a statistically significant but clinically weak association was found, while the top-versus-bottom ACE quartile difference was not statistically significant.

Other supplied passages address hypoglycaemia unawareness with ACE inhibitor/ARB use and ADR-related hospital episodes, not serum ACE and severe hypoglycaemia frequency in Type 1 diabetes.

Yes, reading comprehension ability can be improved in adults with mild intellectual disabilities, based on a study showing substantial transfer effects to general text comprehension after strategy instruction. Yes, adjuvant aromatase inhibitors appear to increase cardiovascular risk compared with tamoxifen in early breast cancer, based on a report of an unexpectedly greater number of grade 3 and 4 cardiovascular events.

Yes, certain preoperative factors are correlated with significant postoperative pain and may help predict it.

Nausea, fever, vomiting, odor, bleeding, otalgia, and trismus were not statistically different between groups, and no ropivacaine-related complications or systemic side effects occurred.
Yes, surgical management appears necessary because viable germ cell elements were found in 14% of testicular remnants from patients with vanishing testes syndrome.

In a retrospective review of 56 patients (age 11–216 months) who had spermatic vessels and a vas deferens exiting a closed internal inguinal ring, 8 of 56 specimens (14%) contained viable germ cell elements, and an additional 4 (7%) had seminiferous tubules without germ cell elements.

Yes, body diffusion-weighted MR imaging is helpful in detecting uterine endometrial cancer when added to nonenhanced MR imaging.

In 23 patients, T2-weighted imaging alone detected endometrial cancer in 19 of 23 (83% sensitivity), and adding DW images and fused DW/T2-weighted images identified cancers in 3 of the remaining 4 patients, increasing overall detection sensitivity to 96%.
The mean ADC value of endometrial cancer was also significantly lower than that of normal endometrium, myometrium, leiomyoma, and adenomyosis (p<0.05).

Yes, pectins appear to be involved in cold acclimation and de-acclimation of winter oil-seed rape, based on cold-induced increases in cell wall and pectin contents and low-methylated pectin, with de-acclimation reversing most of these effects except pectin methylesterase activity.
The study used leaves of two double-haploid winter oil-seed rape (Brassica napus subsp. oleifera) lines differing in winter survival and blackleg resistance.

Cold acclimation at 2 degrees C retarded leaf expansion and increased freezing resistance, tensile stiffness, cell wall and pectin contents, pectin methylesterase activity, and low-methylated pectin independently of genotype.
De-acclimation promoted leaf expansion and reversed most cold-induced effects, except pectin methylesterase activity.

No—the evidence suggests specialised phonological-awareness training is not indicated for every preschool child as a universal intervention, because in a prospective study the whole group showed only a slight difference between specialised phonological-awareness training and general-perception training in later writing abilities.

That study enrolled 218 preschool children and compared 131 after first grade; the specialised program produced the greatest reading benefit specifically in children with a history of hearing loss, actual hearing loss, or pathologic middle-ear findings.

Yes, routine laboratory markers appear useful for distinguishing nonalcoholic from alcoholic steatohepatitis, with a multivariate model including MCV, AST/ALT ratio, and sex achieving an aROC of 0.92.

In 95 biopsy-confirmed steatohepatitis patients (58 NASH, 37 ASH), an AST/ALT ratio >1 was more common in ASH (54.1% vs 20.7%, P=0.0008), and elevated MCV occurred in 53% of ASH patients but was normal in all NASH patients (P<0.0001).

No, low-tone sudden deafness does not inevitably progress to Meniere's disease, based on a retrospective review of 184 patients with low-tone SD.

Among 177 patients with low-tone SD unaccompanied by vertigo, 83 had recurrent hearing loss and only 15 of those 83 developed vertiginous attacks, while 94 had a single episode; among 7 with low-tone SD accompanied by vertigo, 3 had recurrent hearing loss and 2 of those 3 were subsequently confirmed to have Meniere's disease.
No difference in rate of progress from SD to Meniere's disease was observed between low-tone and high-tone SD groups.
The evidence is insufficient to say whether chest wall irradiation should be included after mastectomy in node-negative breast cancer.

The main randomized evidence for postmastectomy locoregional radiation comes from a meta-analysis of 18 trials involving 6,367 patients, but most had node-positive breast cancer treated with modified radical mastectomy; radiation reduced any recurrence (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.58-0.83), local recurrence (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.19-0.34), and mortality (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74-0.94).

The only node-negative study described is a retrospective analysis of 92 internal or central-breast node-negative tumors treated with mastectomy and internal mammary chain irradiation, not chest wall irradiation, and it does not compare outcomes with versus without chest wall irradiation.

In a retrospective immunohistochemical study of 125 HBV-infected patients (25 each with mild, moderate, severe hepatitis, cirrhosis, and HCC) plus 50 additional HBV-related HCCs, c-kit positivity was greatest in severe hepatitis and HCC, and c-kit expression was found in 62 of 75 HCC specimens (82%, p<0.001).
Cirrhotic livers showed lower staining intensity and rare c-kit positivity, while staining intensity paralleled grade and stage in chronic hepatitis B.
However, the passages do not report sensitivity, specificity, or comparisons with other diagnostic markers, so they do not show whether c-kit has diagnostic utility.
Yes, the evidence indicates that the Supplemental Security Income program reduces disability in the elderly, based on a study finding that higher SSI benefits are linked to lower disability rates.

In that study of single individuals aged 65 and older, using 1990 and 2000 censuses and state/year fixed-effect models, an increase of $100 per month in the maximum SSI benefit caused the rate of mobility limitations to fall by 0.46 percentage points, from a baseline of 30%.
The findings were robust to sensitivity analyses, including larger effects among those most likely to receive SSI and no measurable effect among those least likely.

No; the only relevant supplied study found that confined placental mosaicism (CPM) was not increased in IVF/ICSI pregnancies, so it does not support CPM as an explanation for adverse perinatal outcomes.

In a multi-centre retrospective analysis of chorionic villus sampling results, CPM incidence was 1.3% in the IVF/ICSI group versus 2.2% in controls (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.19–1.85), a non-significant difference.
