Multiple regression controlling for age, baseline NIHSS, time to treatment, hypertension, and blood glucose showed no sex difference in recanalization, time to recanalization, or poor 3-month outcome.
The other passages mention sex as a covariate or note prior conflicting literature but report no sex-specific rt-PA effect.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether local anesthesia is needed for MR arthrography of the shoulder.
In one survey of 74 patients, those receiving local anesthetics (n=36) had a mean VAS pain score of 20.8 versus 19.3 for those who did not (n=38), with no significant difference (P=0.83).
A second study randomized 249 patients to local anesthesia (n=61) or no local anesthesia (n=92 and n=96), but the supplied passages do not report its pain results.
Therefore, while one study suggests local anesthesia may not be necessary, the available evidence does not definitively settle the question.

Yes, the SYNTAX score predicts in-hospital outcomes in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI, with independent prediction shown for no-reflow and unadjusted associations with mortality and re-infarction. In 538 STEMI patients undergoing pPCI, those with high SYNTAX score (>22) versus low (<22) had more no-reflow (41% vs 25.1%, p<0.001), lower ejection fraction (38.2±7.5% vs 44.6±8.8%, p<0.001), and higher in-hospital re-infarction (9.5% vs 7.3%, p=0.037) and mortality (0.9% vs 0.2%, p=0.021). On multivariate analysis, SYNTAX score was an independent predictor of no-reflow (OR 1.081, 95% CI 1.032-1.133, p=0.001), but independent prediction of mortality or re-infarction was not reported.
No — AED prescription claims did not show a statistically significant change in trend following the FDA suicidality warning.

In 9,289 Oklahoma Medicaid members with epilepsy and/or psychiatric disorder and at least one AED claim, the prewarning period had a significant upward trend of 0.01% per month (99% CI 0.008%–0.013%, p<0.0001).

Compared with the prewarning trend, no significant change was detected during the warning (change -20.0%, 99% CI -70.0% to 30.0%, p=0.34) or after it (change 80.0%, 99% CI -20.0% to 200.0%, p=0.03), and no stratified diagnostic group had a significant trend change (p>0.01).
The other supplied passages do not address AED prescription claims after the FDA warning.
No; in 42 hypovascular hepatocellular lesions diagnosed by CT arteriography, DWI signal intensity did not significantly predict development of vascularization.
The 730-day cumulative developments of vascularization were 17% for hypointense, 30% for isointense, and 40% for hyperintense lesions, and these differences were not statistically significant.

Yes, ethnicity is associated with where people with cancer die; among 93,375 cancer decedents aged 65 years or older in London from 2001-2010, country of birth as a proxy for ethnicity was associated with place of death after adjustment. Compared with UK-born decedents, hospital deaths were more likely for those born in Asia (proportion ratio 1.12, 95% CI 1.08-1.15) and Africa (PR 1.11, 95% CI 1.07-1.16). Hospice deaths were less likely for those born in Asia (PR 0.73, 95% CI 0.68-0.80), Africa (PR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74-0.93), and other regions (PR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82-0.98), while home deaths were less likely for those born in the Caribbean (PR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85-0.98).

No—concomitant anterior/apical repair during midurethral sling did not improve the overactive bladder symptom component of mixed urinary incontinence more than sling alone in a retrospective cohort. In 151 women with bothersome mixed urinary incontinence, 67 underwent midurethral sling only and 84 underwent midurethral sling plus anterior/apical repair, with the Overactive Bladder Questionnaire Symptom Severity score change measured 6 weeks after surgery. The OAB-q SS change score was 30 ± 26 for sling-only versus 25 ± 25 for sling plus anterior/apical repair (p = 0.20), and multivariate regression showed no difference between groups, indicating similar improvements in OAB symptoms. Thus, the passages show no additional OAB benefit from concomitant repair, although lower change scores were associated with postoperative complications.

No—parent-adolescent emotional closeness, family conflict, and parental permissiveness did not moderate the association between pubertal stage and recent alcohol use in young adolescents. In a cross-sectional survey of 7,631 adolescents aged 10–14 from 231 Australian schools, the interaction of family factors and pubertal stage did not improve the fit of a two-level logistic regression model, so a main-effect model was adopted. That model found significant main effects of pubertal stage only, with boys in middle puberty and girls in advanced puberty at increased odds of alcohol use.
No, HIF1A polymorphisms rs11549465 and rs11549467 were not significantly associated with age-related macular degeneration in the study.
In 87 AMD patients (45 wet, 42 dry) and 80 healthy controls from Turkey, the genotype distributions of these HIF1A SNPs did not differ significantly between cases and controls.
The only significant association found was for CFH rs1061170, where at least one C allele increased AMD risk (OR 2.42, 95% CI 1.22-4.81).

The evidence is mixed/insufficient to say whether pediatric concussion patients are generally compliant with discharge instructions, because the relevant study was designed to evaluate compliance but did not report an overall compliance rate.

In a prospective cohort of 150 patients aged 8 to 17 years discharged from a pediatric ED with concussion, 39% reported return to play on the day of injury, and physician follow-up was 58% at 2 weeks and 64% at 4 weeks.

Among those who had returned to activity at 2 weeks (44%), 35% were symptomatic and 58% did not receive medical clearance; among those returned at 4 weeks (64%), 23% were symptomatic and 54% received medical clearance.
These findings suggest some noncompliance with return-to-play/clearance instructions, but they do not provide a direct overall measure of compliance.

Yes, the evidence supports that assessing joint line positions by means of the contralateral knee is a viable approach for planning knee revision surgery, based on a study where the mean difference in fibular head-to-joint-line distance between treated and control knees was 0.0 mm (95% CI -1.1 to 1.1).

In 100 patients (200 knees, 50 men and 50 women), two independent observers measured distances from bony landmarks to the joint line on scaled weight-bearing anteroposterior radiographs of both knees.
The hypothesis was that joint lines can be directly assessed using the contralateral knee, but only the fibular head result is explicitly reported, so support is strongest for that landmark.
Yes, some mental health differences exist between Francophones and non-Francophones in Manitoba, though the evidence is mixed across indicators.

In a study comparing these groups using administrative and survey data, outside urban areas Francophones had lower rates of diagnosed substance use disorder (rate ratio [RR] = 0.80; 95% CI 0.68 to 0.95) and of suicide and suicide attempts (RR = 0.59; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.79) than non-Francophones.

However, no provincial differences were found for diagnosed mood disorders, anxiety disorders, dementia, or any mental disorders after adjusting for age, sex, and geographic area, while surveyed Francophones were less likely than non-Francophones to report excellent, very good, or good mental health (66.9% vs 74.2%).
Thus, differences appear for specific outcomes and self-rated mental health but not for several diagnosed conditions.
Yes, a retrospective case-control study found that failures of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) were associated with steeper posterior tibial slopes (PTS).
In 20 ACLR failure cases and 20 randomly selected controls from 238 patients, the odds ratio for ACLR failure was 6.8 for medial PTS ≥5° (P=0.007) and 10.8 for lateral PTS ≥5° (P=0.000).
The passage reports mean medial PTS of 3.5° vs.
6.1° and lateral PTS of 2.9° vs.
5.5° for failure vs. control groups, which appear reversed relative to the stated conclusion, but the overall findings support an association.
The evidence is mixed: after BMI screening, parents of overweight children usually recalled their child's weight status but generally did not accurately understand what the measurements meant.

In a randomized trial, 271 overweight children aged 4-8 were screened and 244 parents (90%) were interviewed 2 weeks later; overall recall was 39% of information (mean 6.3 of 16), 94% correctly recalled weight status, but fewer than 10 parents could accurately describe what the measurements meant.
Feedback via best practice care produced slightly better recall than motivational interviewing (difference in total score 0.48; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.92).
Other supplied studies address weight misperception and maternal weight perception, not recall or understanding after screening.
The evidence is insufficient to answer the full question: the supplied data support that sternal fractures are rare in growing children but do not establish that they are often overlooked.
In one study, 4 children aged 5-14 years with sternal fracture were treated over 2 years, with 2 hospitalized for pain management and 2 managed as outpatients.
The same report aimed to investigate detection by radiological and sonographical criteria but provides no results on missed or overlooked fractures.
Other supplied passages address pediatric forearm/distal radius fractures and bone densitometry, not sternal fractures.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that government assistance improves utilization of eye care services by low-income individuals, based on the relevant Canadian study. That study found that government-funded low-income vision care programs exist, but assistance fully covers a general/routine eye examination in only 5 provinces and is inadequate for eyeglasses in 5 provinces, requiring out-of-pocket copayments. Among middle-aged whites without glaucoma, cataracts, diabetes, or vision problems not corrected by lenses, eye care utilization was 28.1% among those with financial difficulty versus 41.9% among those without (p<0.05), adjusted PR 0.68 (95% CI 0.57-0.80). The other two passages address ED utilization and general health care utilization by socioeconomic status, not eye care.
Yes, there is discordance between clinical pathologists and clinicians in reporting and interpreting RBC morphology, based on a survey of 1662 clinicians and 82 clinical pathologists.

Both groups agreed on the usefulness of some terms such as agglutination and correctly interpreted terms such as Heinz bodies, but only clinical pathologists considered other terms such as ghost cells useful, and some clinicians misinterpreted eccentrocytes.

Discordance also appeared in expectations about smear review: 28% of clinicians thought clinical pathologists review all blood smears, whereas only 19% of clinical pathologists reported reviewing all smears.
Thus the passages show discordance in RBC morphology reporting and interpretation between these groups.

Yes, the evidence supports that the inverse equity hypothesis applies to cancer screening coverage in middle-income countries, based on a study of four such countries where economic inequalities in screening were substantially lower or non-existent in countries with higher aggregate coverage. In China, Mexico, Russia, and South Africa (WHO SAGE 2007-2010), breast cancer screening coverage ranged from 10.5% in South Africa to 43% in Mexico, and cervical cancer screening coverage ranged from 24% in South Africa to 81.5% in Russia. The Relative Index of Inequality for breast screening fell from 14.57 in South Africa to 1.04 in Russia, and for cervical screening from 3.60 in China to 1.12 in Russia, showing that inequalities were lower or absent in higher-coverage countries.
No—the best available evidence from the supplied passages indicates that timing of initial surfactant treatment has little or no impact on chronic lung disease (CLD) or mortality after adjustment.

In 2,170 premature infants born at 22–32 weeks’ gestation in Australian NICUs, early surfactant (within 1 hour of birth) versus late surfactant was compared: unadjusted CLD/mortality was higher with early treatment (40.2% vs 20.0%), but the early group was less mature, and multivariable analysis showed little or no impact on CLD/mortality.
Other data show wide variation in surfactant timing but do not provide outcome results for CLD or mortality, so they do not settle the question.
The evidence is insufficient to establish that vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency is related to the development of osteochondritis dissecans.

In a prospective pilot study of 23 consecutive patients (12 male, 11 female) with stage III or III/IV OCD lesions and a mean age of 31.3 years, 18 of 23 had a distinct vitamin D3 deficiency, 2 were vitamin D3-insufficient, and 3 had the lowest normal vitamin D3 value.
However, the study had no control group, so it does not show that vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency contributes to OCD development.

The evidence is mixed but does show correlations between some androgens and sexual desire in women, since a cross-sectional study found sexual desire correlated overall with free testosterone and androstenedione in 560 healthy women aged 19-65.

In the subgroup aged 25-44 with no systemic hormonal contraception, sexual desire correlated with total testosterone, free testosterone, androstenedione, and DHEAS, while in women aged 45-65 only androstenedione correlated.
No correlation was found between ADT-G and sexual desire.

The same report notes that the correlation between circulating androgens and sexual desire is inconclusive and that androgen substitution improves sexual function in women with decreased desire due to surgical menopause, pituitary disease, or age-related ovarian androgen decline.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether the content and presentation of participant information sheets influence recruitment and participation for an antenatal intervention.

One study manipulated the title and font of participant information sheets for pregnant women (n=35) and trainee midwives (n=36), finding that pregnant women rated the Double Awkward condition as significantly more complex than Double Fluent (p=.024) and Awkward Title-Fluent Font (p=.021) conditions.
That study assessed perceptions (Attractiveness, Complexity, Expected Risk, Required Effort) rather than actual recruitment or participation.
Other supplied studies concern a written information sheet for consent recall or medication handouts, not antenatal recruitment or participation.
Yes, bone thickness and inter-radicular space can affect miniscrew placement in posterior mandibular sites; a CBCT study measured these variables and found bone thickness varied with insertion angle.

In 100 orthodontic patients (61 female, 39 male; mean age 17.4 ± 6.74 years; 60 Class I and 40 Class II molar relationships), inter-radicular space was evaluated 5 mm from the cement-enamel junction and bone thickness was simulated at 45°, 60°, and 90° insertion angles.
Inter-radicular space ranged from 2.46 to 3.31 mm and alveolar bone thickness ranged from 8.01 to 13.77 mm, with thickness decreasing as the insertion angle increased from 45° to 90°.
No significant differences were found between genders or malocclusion types.

The evidence is mixed: in a population-based cohort of 1,100 randomly sampled Saskatchewan adults, neck pain was associated with worse physical health-related quality of life (HRQoL) but not mental HRQoL 6 months later.

Compared with participants without neck pain at baseline, those with mild (β=-1.53, 95% CI -2.83 to -0.24), intense (β=-3.60, 95% CI -5.76 to -1.44), or disabling (β=-8.55, 95% CI -11.68 to -5.42) neck pain had worse physical HRQoL after adjustment.
No association was found between neck pain and mental HRQoL, and worsening or persistent neck pain was associated with worse physical HRQoL.

The evidence is mixed: upper airway surgery significantly lowered total cholesterol and lipoprotein(a) in OSA patients, but overall did not change HDL, LDL, or triglycerides. In a retrospective review of 113 adults with OSA who underwent nasal or UPPP surgery, serum TC decreased from 4.86±0.74 to 4.69±0.71 and LP(a) median decreased from 18.50 to 10.90 (P<0.01 and 0.01), with no significant changes in HDL, LDL, or TG (P>0.05). Subgroup effects varied: UPPP patients (n=51) had improvements in TC, HDL, and LP(a), nasal surgery patients (n=62) had only LP(a) decrease, and mixed hyperlipidemia patients had TC and LDL decreases.
No, only a minority of elderly patients correctly endorsed calling 911 for clinical scenarios suggestive of acute stroke.

In a cross-sectional study of 367 elderly out-patients (≥60 years) in Buenos Aires, only 14% correctly endorsed intention to call 911 on the Stroke Action Test (cut-off ≥75%), and only 65% reported they would call an ambulance for the most typical stroke signs and symptoms.
On average, the correct response was chosen only 37% of the time, and the least-recognized symptom (amaurosis fugax) prompted calling in just 15%.
The other supplied passages are methods sections from different studies and do not address this question [PMID:9460489, PMID:12546612].
Yes, plate clearing is positively associated with higher BMI and may be a risk factor for obesity, based on a US cohort study showing an independent positive association.

In 993 US adults (60% male, 80% American European, mean age 31), greater habitual plate clearing was associated with higher BMI after accounting for demographic and behavioral predictors (β=0.18, 95% CI 0.07–0.29, P<0.001).
The other supplied passages do not address plate clearing; they concern obesity as a risk factor for postoperative hypoxia and for GERD/OSA.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that transcranial direct current stimulation can differentiate unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS) from minimally conscious state (MCS).

In 25 severe DOC patients and 20 healthy controls, baseline electrophysiology showed partial preservation of cortical effective connectivity and excitability in MCS but absence in UWS, whereas anodal tDCS over orbitofrontal cortex boosted connectivity/excitability in all healthy controls and MCS patients and unmasked it in some UWS patients.
Thus tDCS may reveal residual connectivity in some UWS, but the passages do not report differentiation accuracy or show that tDCS itself distinguishes UWS from MCS.
Yes.

In a retrospective review of 70 children (17 boys, 53 girls; mean age 5.9 years) with primary VUR (37 grade III, 33 grade IV) treated with endoscopic Macroplastique injection, distal ureteral diameter (UD) and UD ratio were tested as predictors of reflux resolution.
Mean distal UD was 5.5 mm and mean UDR was 37.8%, and both UD and UDR were significant predictors of reflux resolution on logistic regression (P <.007 and P =.001, respectively).
Thus, the supplied evidence indicates distal ureteral diameter can predict reflux resolution after endoscopic injection in this pediatric population.

The evidence is mixed: loss of DKK3 is associated with lymph node metastasis in gastric cancer, and adding DKK3 status to CT improved prediction of lymph node involvement from 71.5% to 80.0% in advanced gastric cancer, but the study assessed DKK3 on gastrectomy specimens rather than preoperative samples.
In 158 gastric cancer patients who underwent gastrectomy, loss of DKK3 expression was found in 64 (40.5%) and was significantly associated with lymph node metastasis (p<0.001).
Based on preoperative CT staging, the combination of DKK3 expression status and CT increased accuracy for predicting lymph node involvement in AGC patients.
However, because DKK3 expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry on surgical samples, these data do not directly demonstrate that preoperative DKK3 testing can predict lymph node metastasis.

The evidence suggests a limited role for MRI in preoperative locoregional staging of gastric cancer, because it had high specificity but lower sensitivity than EUS and did not improve sensitivity when added to MDCT or EUS.

In 52 patients with biopsy-proven gastric cancer, MRI (1.5-T) was compared with 64-channel MDCT and EUS; for T staging, EUS sensitivity was 94% versus 76% for MRI and 65% for MDCT (p=0.08 for MRI vs EUS), while MRI specificity was 89% versus 60% for EUS (p=0.003) and 91% for MDCT.
For N staging, EUS sensitivity was 92% versus 69% for MRI and 73% for MDCT (p=0.01 for MRI vs EUS), and MDCT specificity was 81% versus 73% for MRI (p=0.15) and 58% for EUS (p=0.03).
Adding MRI to MDCT or EUS did not result in significant differences for sensitivity.
Yes, gingival crevicular blood appears reliable for assessing blood glucose level, based on a very strong correlation with finger-prick blood in patients with chronic periodontitis.

In 75 patients (43 males and 32 females) with chronic periodontitis, blood oozing from gingival crevices of anterior teeth after periodontal probing was collected and compared with simultaneous finger-prick blood glucometry.
Patient glucose values ranged from 74 to 256 mg/dl, and the comparison showed a very strong correlation with a t value of 3.97 at P = 0.001.

Yes—TLI assessed in late childhood predicted suicidal behavior from preadolescence through young adulthood, and it was significantly associated with the number and severity of lifetime suicide attempts.
The evidence comes from a longitudinal study of 500 males: 250 sons of men with a lifetime history of substance use disorder and 250 sons of men with no such history.
TLI was measured at baseline age 10–12, and the study hypothesized that it would predict number and severity of suicide attempts.
The reported result supported this by showing TLI was significantly associated with lifetime suicide attempts.

The evidence is insufficient to say whether clinical supervision can sustain the workforce in the current healthcare landscape, because the relevant supplied study assessed perceived supervision effectiveness rather than workforce sustainability.

In a cross-sectional survey of 82 community allied health workers, longer supervision sessions, more sessions, and longer total supervision duration were positively correlated with higher Manchester Clinical Supervision Scale-26 effectiveness scores, and receiving supervision, having some choice of supervisor, and having a completed supervision agreement were associated with higher total scores.
That study did not measure retention, turnover, or workforce sustainability.
Another supplied passage only notes an expected future general surgical workforce shortage and does not test clinical supervision as a remedy.

No, the probability of prenatal diagnosis (PND) or termination of pregnancy for fetal anomaly (TOPFA) does not differ significantly between ART-conceived and spontaneously conceived fetuses with congenital heart defects.

In a population-based study of fetuses with CHD in Paris, PND was 28.1% for ART-conceived (n=171) versus 34.6% for spontaneously conceived (n=4620) fetuses (P=0.077), and TOPFA was 36.2% versus 39.2% (P=0.677), with similar estimates after adjustment for confounders.
Gestational age at PND tended to be earlier for ART fetuses (23.1 vs 24.8 weeks, P=0.05) but was not statistically different after adjustment, and gestational age at TOPFA was comparable.
The other supplied passage does not address PND or TOPFA.
The evidence is insufficient to definitively establish high-IQ schizophrenia as a clinically distinct subtype, although high-IQ patients show some distinguishing clinical features.

In a study of 29 schizophrenia patients with exceptionally high pre-morbid IQ (mean estimated IQ 120), about half had minimal post-onset IQ decline; compared with typical-IQ schizophrenia patients, they had significantly lower negative and disorganised symptoms (RRR=0.019; 95% CI=0.001–0.675, P=0.030) and better global functioning and insight (RRR=1.082; 95% CI=1.020–1.148; P=0.009), while those with minimal decline showed more manic symptoms (RRR=8.213; 95% CI=1.042–64.750, P=0.046).

Other supplied evidence links cognition and schizophrenia genetically and phenotypically (intelligence genetic variance 0.66; phenotypic covariance -0.38, with 89% shared genetic effects) but does not compare high-IQ subtypes, so the passages do not settle whether this is a distinct subtype.
Yes, Web-based and clinic samples of gay men living with HIV differed on self-reported psychological symptoms but not on physical symptoms.

In a London comparison of 154 Web-recruited and 400 clinic-recruited gay men living with HIV, the Web sample had worse mean psychological symptom burden (1.61, SD 1.09 vs 1.36, SD 0.96) and was significantly more likely to be in the worst psychological symptom tertile after adjustment (adjusted OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.41-3.44, P=.001).
Physical symptom burden was similar (mean 0.78, SD 0.65 vs 0.70, SD 0.74), and recruitment setting was not significantly associated with high physical symptom score in multivariable analysis.
The evidence is insufficient to call this a validated improvement of NF EN 13727; the study only suggests adapted trial conditions for antiseptics in the presence of interfering substances.

In vitro, three antiseptic solutions were tested: chlorhexidine-benzalkonium (CB), hexamidine-chlorhexidine-chlorocresol (HCC), and povidone iodine (P), at 97%, 50%, 10%, and 1% concentrations, expecting ≥5 log reduction after 60 seconds.

CB achieved >5 log reduction on all four bacterial strains at 97%, 50%, and 10%; HCC showed bactericidal activity only against P. aeruginosa at 97%; and P was not bactericidal against E. hirae at any concentration or S. aureus at 97%.

The evidence is mixed: trained emergency physicians using the STANDING tool achieved high sensitivity and specificity and good inter-observer agreement for central acute vertigo, but routine ED nystagmus documentation rarely allowed meaningful localization and often conflicted with the final peripheral vestibular diagnosis.

In a single academic ED, five trained EPs with limited nystagmus experience evaluated 98 adults with isolated vertigo against senior audiologist evaluation; central vertigo was suspected in 16 (16.3%), with 13 true positives, 3 false positives, 81 true negatives, and 1 false negative, yielding sensitivity 92.9% and specificity 96.4%, and the whole STANDING test had kappa 0.76.

In contrast, among 1,091 routine dizziness visits, 887 (81.3%) documented a nystagmus assessment, but nystagmus was present in only 185 (20.9%); documentation allowed a meaningful inference in just 10/185 (5.4%), and the nystagmus description conflicted with the EP diagnosis in 113/140 (80.7%) visits given a peripheral vestibular diagnosis.
Thus, accuracy and reliability appear achievable with a structured tool and training, but routine practice assessments are often inadequate.

Yes, the evidence supports that minimally invasive mitral valve repair with artificial chords is reproducible and applicable in routine surgery: in a retrospective review of 426 consecutive patients undergoing minimally invasive video-assisted mitral valve repair, neochords were used in all patients and the repair rate was 99.8%.
Postoperatively, 15 patients (3.5%) had grade I regurgitation and the remainder had none, with 25% extubated in the operating theatre and the rest within 6 hours.
During 3-60 months of follow-up, all patients remained with no or trace mitral regurgitation, and there was no de-insertion or rupture of any neochords and no reoperation.
There were 5 deaths within 30 days (1.2%).
This was a single-arm retrospective review, so it does not provide a direct comparison with other repair techniques.
Yes, certain preresidency selection criteria predict some measures of orthopaedic surgery residency performance, but the evidence comes from a single-institution study of 60 residents.

In that study, ABOS Part I scores correlated moderately with USMLE Step 2 scores (r = 0.55, p<0.001) and number of clinical honors (r = 0.45, p<0.001), while OITE scores correlated weakly with clinical honors (r = 0.35, p = 0.009) and USMLE Step 2 scores (r = 0.29, p = 0.02).
For subjective outcomes, Alpha Omega Alpha membership was associated with higher global evaluation scores (p = 0.005) and correlated with them (r = 0.60, p = 0.005).
The study does not establish that all preresidency criteria predict performance, and its generalizability is limited.

Yes, nasal tip sensation returns after microfat grafting. In a prospective study of 30 young women (age 20.04 ± 3.63 years), nasal tip sensation was assessed objectively and subjectively after microfat injections. The preoperative mean touch threshold was 3.60 units; one week after injection it decreased by 2.50 units, then recovered gradually (1.51 units at week 2, 2.39 at week 4, 3.01 at week 8, and 3.35 at week 12), and the percentage with paresthesia diminished to none, with significant differences across measurement points (P<.05).
Yes—one NICU sustained a zero CLABSI rate for >600 days after a brief recurrence.

In the Tufts Medical Center NICU, adopting standardized care practices including bundles and checklists reduced the CLABSI rate to zero for >370 consecutive days in 2012, and after a first-quarter 2013 increase to 3.3 per 1000 line days, interventions maintained zero for >600 days.
Overall rates fell from 4.1 per 1000 line days in 2009 (13 infections/3163 line days) to 0.94 in 2013 (2 infections/2115 line days), a 77% reduction over 5 years.
Ongoing training, surveillance, and vigilance with insertion and maintenance practices and improved documentation were identified as key drivers, though this is a single-center NICU experience.
No, arch form does not appear to be influenced by sagittal molar relationship or Bolton tooth-size discrepancy.
In 230 Saudi orthodontic patients, pretreatment mandibular casts were classified into tapered, ovoid, or square arch forms, and Bolton ratio and Angle classification were assessed.
No association was observed between significant Bolton discrepancy and sagittal molar relationship or arch form, and no single arch form was significantly more common.
These findings indicate that arch form is not influenced by these factors.
Yes, the high 30-day and 1-year mortality rates after emergency general surgery laparotomy indicate an area of concern and need for improvement.

In a retrospective study of 446 patients (477 laparotomies), 30-day mortality was 12.4% in patients aged <70 years and 22% in those >70 years, and 1-year mortality was 25.15% in those <70 years and 38% in those >70 years (p<0.001 for both comparisons).
The authors concluded that these findings should encourage prospective data collection, improvement of care, and strategies to establish best practice.
No, estradiol + antagonist pretreatment prior to microdose leuprolide did not improve IVF outcomes in poor responders compared with oral contraceptive pill pretreatment.
In a retrospective study of 130 poor responders undergoing IVF with either OCP/ML or E2+antag/ML, ongoing pregnancy rates were significantly higher in the OCP/ML group (40% vs.
There were no significant differences in gonadotropin requirement, cancellation rate, or number of embryos transferred, and trends toward more oocytes retrieved (7.7 ± 3.4 vs.
5.9 ± 4.2) and improved implantation (20% vs.
12%) did not reach statistical significance.

The evidence is indirect but supportive: a national survey of Canadian Royal College emergency medicine residents and program directors found no mandatory active outcome feedback for admitted or discharged patients (0/21 programs). Follow-up was elective for 89.4% of residents for admitted patients and 44.2% for discharged patients, while 76.9% of residents believed follow-up should be mandatory versus 42.9% of program directors (p=0.002). Residents rated the educational value of outcome feedback higher than program directors (5.8/7 vs 5.1/7, p=0.002), suggesting an unmet educational demand that could be leveraged for deliberate practice. However, the survey did not measure deliberate practice or skill outcomes, so it cannot confirm that outcome feedback actually applies that theory.
Yes—sublingual varices were associated with hypertension in an observational study of 431 dental patients.

Grade 1 (medium/severe) sublingual varices were associated with hypertension (OR=2.25, p<0.002), and mean systolic blood pressure was 132 vs 123 mmHg and diastolic 83 vs 80 mmHg for grade 1 vs grade 0.
Sublingual varices indicated hypertension with a positive predictive value of 0.5 and a negative predictive value of 0.80.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that biofeedback training of psychophysiological responses enhances athletes' sport performance; the only relevant study showed improved psychophysiological control but did not report sport performance outcomes.

That study included 18 competitive athletes (4 women, 14 men) in the experimental group and 21 athletes (4 women, 17 men) in the control group, aged 16-34, and found significantly better control of some parameters such as GSR after stress (p=0.037) and heart rate after the STROOP stressor (p=0.037).
However, its results addressed only psychophysiological control, while follow-up questioning about subsequent athletic performance enhancement was described but no performance outcomes were reported.
Other supplied passages address cognitive multitasking in athletes, anal sphincter biofeedback, or physical qualities and sports performance, and do not answer this question.

No, unenhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MRI did not reliably differentiate bone infarcts from acute osteomyelitis in children with sickle cell disease, because bone marrow signal intensity was not significant between groups (P = 0.56).

In a retrospective series of 31 children with SCD and acute bone pain (20 boys, 11 girls; mean age 10.6 years, range 1.1–17.9 years), the clinical standard classified 5 as osteomyelitis and 26 as bone infarct.
The pediatric radiologist classified patients by T1-W fat-saturated signal, but this did not significantly differentiate the diagnoses, and no additional unenhanced MRI parameters proved reliable.
Yes, the clinical presentation of a prior spontaneous preterm birth predicts risk in a subsequent pregnancy, based on a retrospective cohort of 522 singleton pregnancies.
Recurrent preterm birth occurred in 55.2% of women with prior advanced cervical dilatation versus 27.2% with prior preterm premature rupture of membranes and 32.2% with prior preterm labor (P =.001).
Mean gestational age at delivery was also lower after prior advanced cervical dilatation (34.0 weeks) than after PPROM (37.2 weeks) or PTL (37.0 weeks) (P =.001).
Yes, but only partially: rapid prescreening (RPS) flagged 39 of 107 (36.4%) Pap smears with glandular cell abnormalities (≥AGC) among 80,565 smears.
Among 71 patients with histologic follow-up, 24 had high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or carcinoma, and 13 of those 24 (54.2%) were flagged on RPS.
Notably, 11 AGC cases were detected by RPS only and missed by full screening, including 2 with endometrial adenocarcinoma.

The evidence is mixed: in a randomized trial of elective cardiac surgery patients, nurse-led preoperative education reduced anxiety, but its effect on postoperative complications is not clearly settled by the supplied passages.

In 395 patients (205 intervention, 190 control), state anxiety on the day before surgery decreased only in the intervention group (34.0 vs 36.9; P=0.001), and the mean decrease in state anxiety over follow-up was greater in the intervention group (P=0.001).

The trial found no significant difference in length of stay or readmission, and although it reported lower chest infection in the intervention group (10 (5.3%) vs 1 (0.5%); P=0.004), the numbers as presented appear to show the opposite, so a postoperative complication benefit is not clearly established.
The other supplied passages address bariatric surgery and do not inform this question.

Yes, financial incentives appear cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £482 per QALY, though uncertainty remains. In a UK NHS analysis alongside an RCT, 612 pregnant women in Glasgow were randomized to usual cessation support plus or minus up to £400 in vouchers contingent on smoking cessation. The incremental cost per quitter at 34-38 weeks was £1127 ($1716), and the lifetime Markov model yielded an incremental cost of £17 and a 0.04 QALY gain, giving £482/QALY ($734/QALY). Probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated uncertainty, particularly about relapse after birth, and the expected value of perfect information was £30 million at a willingness to pay of £30,000/QALY, so further research may be worthwhile. Other supplied studies address persistence of cessation after pregnancy and smoking trends, not cost-effectiveness.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether we can ease the financial burden of colonoscopy.
One study explored supervised trainees performing unsedated colonoscopies because access to screening colonoscopy is limited by the high cost of sedation, but it did not report cost outcomes.
Another tested a combination of faecal tests to prioritize access to colonoscopy, which could reduce unnecessary procedures, but it did not assess financial burden.

A survey found most patients (91%) were willing to pay 300 euros for a prompt colonoscopy while 7% opted to wait 6 months for a free colonoscopy, indicating patients may bear costs rather than easing them.
Thus, the passages suggest potential strategies but do not settle the question.

Yes, pelvic anatomical structures are in danger during arthroscopic acetabular labral repair, based on a cadaveric study in which free drill penetrations caused 14 injuries in 60 penetrations (23.3%). In ten human cadaveric hips (six male, four female) drilled at anterior, anterior-superior, and superior labral zones, no injuries occurred with stopped drill penetrations. The risk of perforation to the pelvic cavity started at 20 mm drill depth, and the mean depth for all insertions was 31.7 mm (SD 2.6). The findings are limited to cadaveric models and do not address clinical outcomes.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether cardiac reoperations benefit octogenarians; the only supplied study of this question reports methods for 84 consecutive patients aged ≥80 years who underwent a cardiac reoperation, with functional status and quality of life to be assessed, but provides no outcomes.

The other supplied passages address different operations in octogenarians, such as isolated CABG in 130 patients (in-hospital mortality 13%, no difference by revascularization completeness) and carotid endarterectomy in 95 patients (no deaths), not cardiac reoperations.
Therefore, the passages do not show whether cardiac reoperations in octogenarians are beneficial or not.
The evidence is mixed but suggests that mammographic density does not independently impact margin re-excision rates after breast-conserving surgery.

In one cohort of 655 patients, denser breasts showed only a bivariable trend toward more frequent re-excision that disappeared in multivariable analysis, and unnecessary margins did not differ by density.
In another cohort of 758 patients, density did not predict margin status or conversion to mastectomy after initial BCS, although initial BCS was less common with the highest density.
Thus, mammographic density may influence surgical choice but does not appear to independently affect margin re-excision rates.
Yes, evidence from a hospital natural experiment indicates that evidence-based practice improved some patient outcomes, specifically lower mortality and shorter length of stay.

In that study, patients treated by EBP doctors in an internal medicine service from 2004-11 had a lower risk of death than standard-practice patients (6.27% vs 7.75%, P < 0.001) and a shorter length of stay (6.01 vs 8.46 days, P < 0.001).

Within the EBP unit, mortality fell from 7.4% to 6.3% (P < 0.02) and length of stay from 9.15 to 6.01 days (P = 0.002), while no statistically significant improvements were seen in standard-practice physicians.
Readmission rates were similar (14.4% EBP vs 14.5% SP), so the improvement was not seen across every outcome.

Other supplied passages do not report EBP outcome results; they address asthma care implementation, surgical volume, patient-centered care, or team-based practice, so the evidence rests on the single natural experiment.
No—among 7 people with type 1 diabetes and 10 controls who regularly ran more than 5 km, no Achilles tendon response to load was seen in either group over the 4 days after a 10 km run.
Baseline tendon structure was similar between groups, including UTC echo-types I–IV and anterior-posterior thickness (all p > 0.05).
Thus, in this small study, type 1 diabetes did not appear to affect Achilles tendon response to a 10 km run.

The evidence is mixed or insufficient for whether phone interviews and clinic self-surveys measure the same thing, because the relevant randomized comparison used mailed self-administered questionnaires rather than in-clinic self-surveys.

In 823 patients with headache (mean age 51.7, 664 women), telephone interviews and mailed questionnaires were equivalent except for the SF-12 mental scales, where self-administered scores were 3.5 points (2.9–4.0) lower than telephone interviews.
Telephone interviews also produced fewer missing data (0.5% vs 2.8%, p<0.001).
Thus, the passages do not settle the clinic self-survey comparison but do show that survey mode can affect mental health PRO scores.

No, the supplied evidence does not show additional value: in 73 GEP-NET patients selected for PRRT based on positive SRS, sst2a IHC was positive in 93% and was not significantly related to best response 1 year after PRRT (p = 0.47).
The study therefore does not support sst2a IHC as an added predictor beyond SRS uptake, although it did not directly compare the predictive performance of the two tests.

Yes, the evidence from one quasi-experimental study suggests teleoncology models can enable safe chemotherapy delivery in rural towns, with no significant differences in dose intensity or toxicity between rural and tertiary-center patients.

In that study, 89 patients in Mount Isa received 626 chemotherapy cycles under teleoncology supervision, while 117 patients at the Townsville Cancer Centre received 799 cycles, with no significant differences in mean cycles, dose intensities, side-effect proportions, or hospital admissions, and no toxicity-related deaths in either group.

A separate study found rural colon cancer patients had later stage diagnosis, lower chemotherapy receipt for stage III disease, and worse cancer-specific survival, but it did not evaluate teleoncology models or chemotherapy safety.

Yes, a retrospective study found higher serologic evidence of viral infection in patients with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), suggesting viruses may have a role. In that study, 483 BPPV patients were compared with 461 healthy controls, and with the exception of influenza and parainfluenza, all viral serology values (HSV1, HSV2, Herpes zoster, EBV, CMV, adenovirus) were higher in the BPPV group. Seasonal variation was also observed, with elevated values for specific viruses in March, April, May, June, and September, and increased values for all studied viruses in October. However, this evidence comes from a single retrospective study, so it supports but does not definitively establish a viral role in BPPV.

The evidence is insufficient to definitively establish patient-controlled therapy (PCT) as a new therapeutic concept for opioid administration in palliative care, resting on a small uncontrolled pilot study.

In 18 inpatients with advanced disease and refractory breathlessness who received intravenous opioid PCT, median numeric rating scale breathlessness decreased from 5 at baseline (range 1-10) to 4 on Day 1 (range 0-8, P<0.01) and 4 on Day 2 (range 0-5, P<0.01), with stable physiological parameters and 12/12 patients reporting relief on Day 3.
Because this was a pilot observational study without a comparison group, it does not settle whether PCT should be adopted as a new therapeutic concept.
Opioids are first-line for dyspnea but respiratory depression is a feared side effect, so further controlled evaluation is needed.
Yes, some surrogates of injury severity influence the occurrence of heterotopic ossification after acetabular fracture surgery.

In 241 patients treated through a posterior approach with at least 6-month radiographic follow-up, ICU length of stay and non-ICU length of stay greater than 10 days were significantly associated with HO development in multivariate modeling.

Specifically, ICU LOS 1-2 days had OR 4.33 (95% CI 1.03-18.25), 3-6 days had OR 4.1 (95% CI 1.27-13.27), and more than 6 days had OR 11.7 (95% CI 3.24-42.22), while non-ICU LOS greater than 10 days had OR 7.6 (95% CI 2.6-22.25).

However, injury severity score itself and other factors such as age, gender, mechanism of injury, neurologic injury, Letournel fracture type, hip dislocation, interval from injury to surgery, operative time, and estimated blood loss were not significantly associated with HO development or severity.

Yes—limited evidence suggests less is more for a contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion, based on a series where all hydroceles were managed through a scrotal approach without inguinal exploration.

In 37 patients with neonatal torsion (average age 3.5 days), 22 had a contralateral hydrocele; all hydroceles were opened through a scrotal approach at the time of contralateral scrotal fixation, and no patient underwent inguinal exploration for a patent processus vaginalis.
None of those patients developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years (range 4.3–11.2 years) of follow-up.

However, this is a single case series without a comparison group, so it supports safety and effectiveness of the less invasive approach but does not definitively prove superiority over inguinal management.
Evidence is mixed: one matched study found that young colorectal cancer patients have distinct epidemiological and clinicopathological features, but age was not predictive of survival.

In that study of 406 patients (203 aged ≤50 years vs 203 older than 50 years), the younger group showed female predominance, different ethnic composition, more family history of cancer and hereditary CRC syndromes, fewer polyps, and higher rates of left-sided tumors and stage III-IV disease, while age was not a survival predictor.
Other passages state that it remains unclear whether the disease has unique features in young patients and that prognosis and clinicopathologic features continue to be debated.
They describe comparisons of patients aged ≤40 or <40 years with older patients but provide no results, so they do not settle whether young-onset CRC is a distinct clinical entity.

The evidence is mixed: dose-point evaluation at PIBS points tracked planned doses well in one study, but it showed important differences related to vaginal involvement and at the ICRU rectovaginal point.

In 19 cervical cancer patients treated with image-guided brachytherapy after concurrent radiochemotherapy, mean prescribed doses at PIBS -2, PIBS, and PIBS +2 were 2.23 ± 1.4, 6.39 ± 6.6, and 31.85 ± 36.06 Gy.
Delivered doses at the PIBS points did not differ significantly from prescribed doses and correlated strongly with them (R² 0.93–0.95), and applicator movements relative to PIBS were insignificant.

However, patients with vaginal involvement (5) had significantly higher doses than the remaining 14 at PIBS +2 (+47.60 Gy, p=0.023) and PIBS (+7.46 Gy, p=0.03), and delivered dose at the ICRU rectovaginal point was 1.43 ± 2.49 Gy lower than planned (p=0.019).
Other supplied passages concern different cervical/endometrial cancer treatment schedules and do not directly test PIBS vaginal dose-point reliability.

Yes—one study using anchoring vignettes indicates adjustment for reporting heterogeneity is necessary in sleep disorders because it changed which factors were significantly associated with sleep problems.

In 1002 Japanese adults aged 18+, 53% reported sleep/energy problems; before correction age, sex, and number of comorbidities were significantly associated with greater sleep-problem severity, but after correction sex was no longer significant and regular exercise became significant, with only subtle coefficient differences between models.
The other supplied passages address sleep and health outcomes but not reporting heterogeneity, so the evidence rests on that single study.

Mixed: in a prospective single-centre study of 1829 attendances (40.7% admitted), triage nurses' admission probability estimate (VAS) was not better than the objective GAPS score overall, with comparable discrimination (AUC 0.876 for GAPS vs 0.875 for VAS, p=0.93) and accuracy (80.6% vs 79.0%, p=0.18).
However, nurses overestimated admissions (47.3% vs actual 40.7%, p<0.0001), whereas GAPS was well calibrated (41.0%, p=0.678).

In the majority of cases where nurses were not at least 95% certain, GAPS significantly outperformed nurses on calibration (+1.2% vs +9.2%, p<0.0001), discrimination (AUC 0.810 vs 0.759, p=0.001) and accuracy (75.1% vs 68.9%, p=0.0009).

When nurses felt at least 95% certain (a minority), their accuracy was excellent at 92.4%, and a strategy using GAPS but over-ruling it when clinical certainty was ≥95% outperformed either method alone (AUC 0.891, accuracy 82.5%).
Yes—depression diagnosis and antidepressant prescribing varied by neighbourhood ethnic density in a study of over one million GP patients in four London boroughs.
Black and minority ethnic groups were up to four times less likely than white British patients to be newly diagnosed with depression or prescribed antidepressants.

For each 10% increase in own-ethnic density, odds of new depression diagnosis decreased for Pakistani (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70-0.93), Indian (OR 0.88, CI 0.81-0.95), African (OR 0.88, CI 0.78-0.99), and Bangladeshi (OR 0.94, CI 0.90-0.99) patients but increased for Black Caribbean patients (OR 1.26, CI 1.09-1.46), with similar antidepressant-use results except the Black Caribbean effect was not significant (p=0.07).
Yes, a novel vascular-guided multilayer preauricular approach (VMPA) to the temporomandibular joint was associated with successful access and no severe complications in a consecutive case series.

In 606 joints from patients without prior TMJ surgery who were followed at least 6 months, all TMJ surgeries through the VMPA were successful, incisions healed favorably, and no patient developed permanent facial nerve weakness or other severe complications.
However, this study did not directly compare VMPA with other approaches, so it supports but does not prove that this novel approach improves access and reduces complications.

Yes, duplex Doppler ultrasonography can non-invasively diagnose esophageal varices in patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis, based on a splenoportal index (SPI) cutoff of 5.0 that achieved 88% diagnostic accuracy.
In 56 patients with compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class A), duplex Doppler indices were compared with screening endoscopy as the reference standard.

Mean portal vein velocity, splenic index, and SPI predicted esophageal varices (p < 0.05), while hepatic and splenic arterial resistive and pulsatility indices did not (p > 0.05); SPI < 5.0 correctly identified absence in 27/28 patients (96% negative predictive value and sensitivity), and SPI ≥ 5.0 correctly identified presence in 22/28 patients (79% positive predictive value and 82% specificity).
No, septoplasty did not significantly change the dimensions of compensatory middle turbinate hypertrophy.

In patients with nasal septal deviation, radiological measurements of the mucosal and bony middle turbinate components on the concave and convex sides before and at least one year after septoplasty showed no significant changes.

There was a significant negative correlation after septoplasty between the septal angle and middle turbinate total area on the deviated side (p = 0.033), but this does not indicate a change in turbinate dimensions.
The other supplied passages report symptom outcomes after septoplasty and do not address middle turbinate dimensions.
No, the evidence suggests bare-metal stent implantation is not justifiable in high bleeding risk patients when a drug-eluting stent can be used with abbreviated dual antiplatelet therapy.

Among 828 HBR patients randomized to zotarolimus-eluting Endeavor Sprint stent or BMS followed by 30-day DAPT, MACE occurred in 22.6% vs 29% (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57-0.98, p=0.033), with lower MI (3.5% vs 10.4%) and TVR (5.9% vs 11.4%) and reduced stent thrombosis in the DES arm, while bleeding did not differ.

A separate background statement notes DES is the treatment of choice and BMS has only marginal indications, with BMS remaining a candidate mainly for patients with DES contraindications such as inability to sustain 6-12 months of DAPT.
However, the ZEUS protocol used only 30-day DAPT, so the supplied passages support DES over BMS in this HBR setting rather than demonstrating a persistent justification for BMS.

No—the evidence indicates paucigranulocytic asthmatics are not truly non-inflammatory, because they still show increased sputum eosinophils and systemic inflammatory markers compared with healthy subjects.

In a retrospective cross-sectional study of 833 asthmatics vs 194 healthy subjects, sputum eosinophils (absolute and percentage) were increased in all asthma phenotypes including paucigranulocytic asthma (p < 0.005), and all asthma phenotypes had increased blood leukocyte counts, with paucigranulocytic asthmatics also having increased absolute blood eosinophils vs healthy subjects (p < 0.005).

The other supplied passages do not directly compare paucigranulocytic inflammation with healthy subjects, as PMID:21790924 reports phenotype distribution and predictors, and PMID:11555508 describes methods for obstruction/ICS groups and sputum eosinophil counts.
The evidence is insufficient to say whether obesity is a triggering cause of incidentally detected idiopathic misty mesentery.
In a study of 561 patients with misty mesentery on CT, 80 had isolated incidental idiopathic misty mesentery, giving a prevalence of 7%, and 67.5% of all patients were obese and 17.5% overweight.
The study did not include a control group or causal analysis, so these data show an association but cannot establish that obesity triggers the condition.
The other passages concern obesity and OSA/GERD, not misty mesentery.
No, viral co-infection did not influence the severity of acute respiratory infection in children, because the number of detected viruses did not correlate with any markers of severity.

In a Spanish prospective multicenter study of 204 children admitted with ARI, with a UK replication cohort of 97, viral co-infection was assessed by PCR detection of multiple viruses and compared to severity markers, and no correlation was found.

Bacterial superinfection, however, was associated with increased severity (OR 4.356; P=0.005), PICU admission (OR 3.342; P=0.006), higher clinical score (1.988; P=0.002), respiratory support (OR 7.484; P<0.001), and longer hospital stay (OR 1.468; P<0.001).
Yes—LAA occlusion altered ECG and some follow-up echocardiographic parameters in patients with AF, based on a study of 73 patients undergoing Watchman, LAmbre, or Lefort devices.
After LAA occlusion, most patients had a slight measurable QRS axis shift, and there were significant pre- vs post-operative differences in heart rate and mean-mean QT interval.

Immediate echocardiographic parameters did not differ significantly before vs after implantation, but LA diameter was larger at 6 months and aortic root diameter larger at 12 months than preoperative baseline.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that rectal anastomosis in gynaecological debulking surgery without a diverting stoma is safe, because the only gynaecological debulking study supplied does not report anastomotic leakage by stoma status.

In that retrospective study, 43 major colorectal procedures were performed on 37 women during cytoreduction, including 22 low rectal resections, 7 anterior rectal resections, 4 sigmoid resections, 5 Hartmann's procedures, and only 3 diverting loop ileostomies; the primary outcome was anastomotic leakage with or without a diverting stoma, but no outcome results are provided.

Other supplied passages address different populations, including acute perforated diverticulitis , colon and upper rectum anastomosis without defunctioning colostomy in 47 patients of whom 16 were emergency operations , and conservative management of anastomotic leakage after rectal surgery , so they do not establish safety for gynaecological debulking without a diverting stoma.

Yes, flexible instruments can create adequate femoral tunnel lengths at 90° of knee flexion in ACL reconstruction. In a cadaveric study of 10 fresh knees, flexible guide pins were inserted at 70°, 90°, and 120° of flexion and intra-osseous length was measured. Mean intra-osseous length at 90° was 32.1 mm (range 22-45 mm), exceeding the 20-mm adequacy threshold and significantly greater than 25.2 mm (20-32 mm) at 70° (p<0.05). There were no significant differences among groups in distance to the LCL, and distance to the common peroneal nerve trended longer with more flexion, with a significant difference only for 120° vs 70° (p<0.05).

Bottom line: yes, infectious disease experts show substantial but not perfect agreement when assessing appropriateness of antimicrobial prescribing, with specialists matching a modal expert reference standard in 80% of cases and an index expert in 76%.

In 24 infectious disease or clinical microbiology doctors (16 specialists, 8 residents) from five hospitals rating 56 paper cases, criterion validity against the modal assessment of 16 specialists was 80% (range 75%-86%), with sensitivity 75% and specificity 84%; results did not differ by specialty, hospital, or experience, and residents were similar.
Agreement with the index expert was 76%, and the index expert agreed with his own previous assessments in 71% of cases.
The other study evaluated physicians' knowledge and observed antibiotic prescriptions, not agreement among experts, so it does not directly settle expert agreement.
The evidence is mixed/insufficient to conclude that KIT mutation analysis will be a pathfinder for neoadjuvant imatinib in locally advanced GIST.

In 125 patients with locally advanced or locally recurrent GIST treated with neoadjuvant imatinib, only 45 (36%) had c-kit mutation testing; exon 11 was found in 25 (55.5%), exon 9 in 3 (6.7%), exon 13 in 2 (4.4%), 12 were wild type (26.6%), and 3 (6.7%) were uninterpretable.
Exon 11 mutants had a higher response rate than non-exon 11 mutants (84% vs 40%, p=0.01) and a higher disease stabilization rate (92% vs 75%), and 84% vs 75% were surgical candidates.

However, there were no differences between the various exon variants in outcomes and responses, and current longer neoadjuvant imatinib duration is not based on tumor biology reflected by KIT mutation analysis.
No, there is no significant correlation between humeral and glenoidal bony defects in chronic anterior posttraumatic shoulder dislocation.

In a retrospective study of 30 patients (25 men, 5 women, mean age 29.8 years) with chronic posttraumatic anterior instability and bone defects in both the glenoid and humerus, the humeral D/R ratio (mean 23%) and glenoid D1/D2 ratio (mean 95%) were measured.
No significant correlation was found between these defects for either observer (r = 0.23, p = 0.22; r = 0.05, p = 0.78).
A separate study of 36 patients examined only glenoid defect measurement methods and did not assess humeral-glenoid correlation.
Yes, electrochemiluminescence (ECL) assays improved prediction of time to type 1 diabetes in autoantibody-positive TrialNet subjects.
In 1,287 autoantibody-positive TrialNet subjects with available ECL-IAA and ECL-GADA data, 177 developed diabetes after a median follow-up of 24 months.
ECL-positive subjects had a 58% risk of progression to diabetes within 6 years versus 5% for ECL-negative subjects (P<0.0001).

In multivariate Cox models, the model with ECL-GADA and/or ECL-IAA positivity was best, and adding ECL to the Diabetes Prevention Trial risk score improved the receiver operating characteristic curve with an AUC of 0.83 (P<0.0001).
No, the supplied evidence indicates risk calculators are not accurate for predicting surgical site occurrence (SSO) after open ventral hernia repair, with low areas under the curve (AUCs).
In a retrospective multicenter database (n=795; SSO rate 23%), the SSO AUCs were 0.56, 0.54, 0.52, and 0.60 for VHRS, VHWG, CDC wound class, and HW-RAT.
In a prospective single-center database (n=88; SSO rate 14%), the SSO AUCs were 0.63, 0.54, 0.50, 0.57, and 0.69.

Some models did stratify patients into groups with differing SSO rates (VHRS and HW-RAT retrospectively; ACS-NSQIP prospectively), but VHRS, VHWG, and CDC overestimated SSO risk while HW-RAT and ACS-NSQIP underestimated it.

The passages do not settle accuracy for surgical site occurrences outside open ventral hernia repair; one related passage notes that external validation of colorectal surgical site infection prediction models is lacking.
Yes, a qualitative study of MPH programs found considerable reported contributions to health system strengthening in low- and middle-income countries, though with limitations.

In-depth interviews with 10 graduates per program, their peers, and supervisors from a distance MPH program in South Africa and a residential program in the Netherlands reported workplace impacts including promotion to leadership, expanded management roles, workplace innovations, teaching, advocacy, and community engagement.

Beyond the workplace, graduates had national reach through policy advisory roles to Ministries of Health, policy development, and capacity building, but work conditions and context influenced their effect and self-selection and social acceptability bias may have influenced findings.

The evidence is mixed: in a Swedish 10-year longitudinal study (n=744), young adults from abstaining families in 2000 drank substantially less in 2010 than offspring of non-abstaining families, but the difference across quintiles was not statistically significant and actual drinking levels in drinking families were not or only weakly associated with offspring drinking.
This indicates that familial transmission of abstinence may persist into young adulthood, while transmission of drinking quantity-frequency does not clearly persist.

A separate Australian study examined maternal parenting at child age 5 as a predictor of problematic drinking in adolescence, not young adulthood, so it does not settle persistence into young adulthood.
Yes, a randomized controlled trial found that multi-modal cervical physical therapy significantly improved tinnitus complaints in patients with cervicogenic somatic tinnitus.

The study included 38 patients with severe subjective tinnitus (TFI 25–90 points) and neck complaints (NBQ >14 points), randomized to immediate-start therapy (n=19) or 6-week delayed-start therapy (n=19), and all received 6 weeks of cervical physical therapy (12 sessions).
TFI scores decreased significantly after treatment (p=0.04), with 53% reporting substantial improvement immediately after treatment, although this was maintained in only 24% at 6-week follow-up.
The reported improvement is based on within-group changes after treatment rather than a between-group comparison in the supplied passages.

The evidence is mixed: the Catholic bishops' boycott call did not cause a large drop in national polio vaccination coverage, but parental refusal as a reason for missed vaccination increased significantly.
In a cross-sectional survey across 32 Kenyan counties with 90,157 children and 37,732 parents/guardians, national coverage was 93% in August 2015 compared with 94% in November 2014.

The proportion of children not vaccinated due to parental refusal rose from 6% to 12%, while Catholics made up 31% of parents/guardians but only 7% of missed children, and the survey did not directly attribute the refusal increase to the boycott.
No, amblyopia treatment did not normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in this study.

In 32 anisometropic hyperopic children with unilateral amblyopia, mean choroidal thickness was significantly higher in amblyopic eyes than fellow eyes before treatment (p = 0.019), with no significant pre- versus post-treatment change in amblyopic eyes after six months (p = 0.428) or fellow eyes (p = 0.343).

Despite visual acuity improving from 0.35 ± 0.3 to 0.16 ± 0.2 logMAR (p < 0.001), mean choroidal thickness remained significantly higher in amblyopic eyes than fellow eyes after treatment (p = 0.006).

The evidence is mixed: in adolescents aged 15-18, comorbid major depression (MD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) was associated with significantly higher rates of adult MD at ages 18-35 than AUD-only (p<.05) and marginally higher rates than MD-only (p<.10), and all three disorder groups had higher rates than the no-disorder group.

However, after adjustment for confounding by gender, childhood behavior problems, and exposure to physical and sexual abuse, the difference in adult MD rates between the MD-only and comorbid MD/AUD groups was no longer statistically significant.
Thus, comorbidity may indicate poorer depression outcomes, but much of the association appears explained by shared risk factors; the data were self-reported and may be subject to biases.
Yes, the retromandibular transparotid approach appears to be a reliable option for surgical treatment of condylar fractures based on a retrospective series of 25 patients.

In these patients, preinjury occlusion and temporomandibular joint health were restored in most, esthetic outcomes were satisfactory, and there were no permanent neurologic impairments or major postoperative complications.
The study evaluated static and dynamic occlusal function, temporomandibular joint health, neurologic impairments, and esthetic outcomes with a minimum 1-year follow-up.
However, it was a single retrospective evaluation without a reported comparison group, so the evidence supports reliability but does not compare this approach to others.
Yes—the supplied study found that aortic arch anatomy is associated with traumatic aortic injury severity.

In 22 TAI patients treated with TEVAR, mean aortic arch index and angle differed by injury type (type I: 6.8 cm and 58.3°; type III: 4.4 cm and 45.9°; type IV: 3.3 cm and 37°), with substantial differences between type III and IV.
Multivariate analysis confirmed that aortic arch angle was significantly associated with occurrence of type III damage (OR 1.5; 95% CI 1.03–2.2).
This is a small retrospective study, so it supports but does not definitively establish the relationship.
No; in the one relevant study, simultaneous use of an endoscope did not significantly change ventriculoperitoneal shunt infection rates.
Among 438 VPS procedures, infection occurred in 22.4% when an endoscope was used versus 18% when it was not (P=0.449).
In first-time shunt groups rates were 28.6% vs 16.2% (P=0.27), and in revision/second-time groups 20% vs 19.8% (P=0.977).
Yes, non-HDL-C appeared to be a better predictor of long-term MACE than LDL-C in a retrospective study of 868 Thai patients after acute myocardial infarction.

During mean follow-up of 2.6 years, non-HDL-C >130 mg/dl was associated with higher MACE (HR 3.15, 95% CI 1.46-6.80, p=0.003) versus non-HDL-C <100 mg/dl, while LDL-C >100 mg/dl was associated with reduced MACE risk (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.18-0.98, p=0.046) versus LDL-C <70 mg/dl.
This evidence is limited to one retrospective study with a relatively short mean follow-up, and the other supplied passages do not address this comparison.

Yes, with limited evidence: one health care management study found that strategic use of performance measurement systems directly and significantly (p < 0.001) enhanced performance in terms of improved processes.
That finding comes from a PLS analysis of a survey of 97 Italian managers working for health care organizations in the Lombardy region, with a 77.6% response rate.
The same study also reported that perceived managerial discretion was positively and significantly affected by strategic PMS use (p < 0.001), although the mediation effect was non-significant.
Other supplied passages concern performance measures or physical performance rather than testing performance measurement systems as management tools, so they do not settle the broader question.
The evidence suggests that sub-Saharan Africa is not yet well positioned to cope with the ART-related adverse effects expected under the WHO "test and treat" policy.

Implementation of this policy is expected to increase adverse effects such as cardiovascular disease, lipodystrophy, prediabetes and overt diabetes, insulin resistance, and hyperlactatemia/lactic acidosis, and these disorders already have high prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa.

Most sub-Saharan African countries face extreme poverty, weak health systems, inadequate health services, lack of qualified personnel and equipment, and unaffordable medicines, which would hamper management of this added burden.

There is also a dearth of data on the incidence and predictive factors of ART-related adverse effects in the region, limiting the ability to anticipate and plan an adequate response, and no specific quantitative estimates of the upcoming burden or coping capacity are provided.
The other supplied passages address HAART eligibility, transmission impact, and adherence/mortality but do not provide evidence on coping with ART-related adverse effects.
Yes—the first urinary ACR appears to be an independent prognostic factor for maternal and neonatal adverse outcomes in women with suspected preeclampsia.

In 717 singleton pregnancies after 20 weeks referred for suspected preeclampsia, each 1-unit increase in log-transformed first ACR was associated with increased odds of composite adverse maternal outcome (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.45-1.80) and adverse neonatal outcome (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.02-1.29), and with reduced gestational age at delivery (coefficient -0.46, 95% CI -0.54 to -0.38) in multivariable analysis adjusting for existing prognostic factors.
The evidence is limited: a single-level visceral adipose tissue (VAT) area can track changes in VAT volume, but the supplied passages do not show that it represents absolute VAT volume.
